# Module 1 — Random Variables

## 1.1 Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU 2024 Definition (Formal):**
> A **Random Variable (RV)** is a real-valued function defined on a sample space $S$ of a random experiment. Formally, it is a mapping
> $$X : S \to \mathbb{R}$$
> such that every event of the form $\{X \le x\}$ belongs to the $\sigma$-field of the underlying probability space. In KTU-board parlance, the RV converts *non-numerical* outcomes (e.g., a coin toss, a faulty signal) into *numerical* values that we can analyze with calculus and algebra.

In simpler words, a random variable is **NOT a variable that is random** — it is a **function** that *maps* each outcome of an experiment to a number.

### Conceptual Analogy — The "Voltage Meter" Intuition

Imagine you connect a noisy sensor to a digital voltmeter. Every microsecond the voltmeter reads *some* number between **0 V** and **5 V**, but the exact number changes unpredictably. The "voltmeter reading" $X$ is your **random variable**, and the underlying random experiment is the *thermal/agitation noise* inside the sensor.

- The **sample space** $S$ is the set of *all physically possible* outcomes of the noise.
- The **random variable** $X$ is the *translator* — it converts each invisible micro-state into a number on the screen.

So whenever an electrical engineer records a "value," a "current," a "bit error count," or an "SNR in dB," he/she is implicitly working with a random variable.

### Classification of Random Variables (KTU Board-Favourite Tabulation)

| Category | Sub-type | Sample Range | Function Used |
|----------|----------|--------------|---------------|
| Univariate | Discrete | Countable ($x = 0,1,2,\dots$) | Probability Mass Function (PMF) |
| Univariate | Continuous | Any real interval | Probability Density Function (PDF) |
| Bivariate | Joint (Discrete / Continuous) | $\mathbb{R}^2$ | Joint PMF / Joint PDF |

> [!NOTE]
> In **GBMAT401 (Electrical Science stream)**, the syllabus emphasizes **univariate** discrete and continuous RVs and their expectations. Bivariate (joint) distributions appear only as a brief mention in later modules.

### Why Random Variables Matter in Electrical Engineering

- **Signal Processing:** Noise voltages are modeled as continuous RVs (typically Gaussian).
- **Communication Systems:** Bit-error counts in a packet are discrete RVs (Binomial / Poisson).
- **Reliability Engineering:** Time-to-failure of a component is an Exponential RV.
- **Power Systems:** Load demand (in MW) is treated as a continuous RV for load-flow studies.
- **Control Systems:** Stochastic disturbances are modeled as random inputs to LTI systems.

> [!TIP]
> **KTU Examiner Tip:** When asked *"Define a random variable,"* always include **three** things in your answer:
> 1. It is a **function**, not a variable.
> 2. It is defined on a **sample space**.
> 3. It takes **real numerical values**.
> Missing any one of the three costs you a mark.

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->

# 1.2 Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 1.2.1 The Operational Pipeline of a Random Variable

A random variable's "life cycle" in any KTU problem can be broken into five logical steps:

1. **Identify the experiment** — e.g., "Toss 3 fair coins and count heads."
2. **Construct the sample space** $S$ — e.g., $S = \{HHH, HHT, HTH, THH, HTT, THT, TTH, TTT\}$.
3. **Define the RV** — e.g., $X$ = number of heads in the three tosses.
4. **Compute the distribution** — list $P(X = x)$ for every possible $x$ (discrete) or write $f(x)$ (continuous).
5. **Extract moments** — Mean $E(X)$, Variance $V(X)$, and so on.

## 1.2.2 Distribution Functions (PMF, PDF, CDF)

### A. Probability Mass Function (PMF) — Discrete RV

For a discrete RV $X$ taking values $x_1, x_2, \dots$, the PMF is denoted $p_X(x)$ and is defined as

$$p_X(x) = P(X = x)$$

It must satisfy two axioms:

$$p_X(x) \ge 0 \quad \forall x \in \mathbb{R}$$

$$\sum_{\text{all } x} p_X(x) = 1$$

### B. Probability Density Function (PDF) — Continuous RV

For a continuous RV, the PDF $f_X(x)$ is **not** a probability. It is a *density*, meaning

$$P(a \le X \le b) = \int_{a}^{b} f_X(x)\, dx$$

Axioms:

$$f_X(x) \ge 0 \quad \forall x \in \mathbb{R}$$

$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_X(x)\, dx = 1$$

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Board Pitfall:** For a *continuous* RV, $P(X = a) = 0$ for *any* single point $a$. This is one of the most-asked true/false questions in KTU exams.

### C. Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) — Universal

The CDF applies to **both** discrete and continuous RVs and is the single most "universal" object in probability theory.

$$F_X(x) = P(X \le x)$$

Properties of CDF (KTU must-know list):

- $0 \le F_X(x) \le 1$ for all $x$.
- $F_X(x)$ is **non-decreasing**.
- $F_X(-\infty) = 0$ and $F_X(+\infty) = 1$.
- $F_X(x)$ is **right-continuous** (this is a measure-theoretic fact, but KTU questions rarely test it).

Conversion identities:

For **discrete** RV:

$$F_X(x) = \sum_{x_i \le x} p_X(x_i)$$

For **continuous** RV:

$$F_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f_X(t)\, dt$$

Conversely,

$$f_X(x) = \frac{d}{dx} F_X(x) \quad \text{(at points of continuity)}$$

## 1.2.3 Moments — The "Numerical DNA" of an RV

| Moment | Discrete Formula | Continuous Formula | Engineering Meaning |
|--------|------------------|--------------------|---------------------|
| Mean $\mu = E(X)$ | $\sum x \, p_X(x)$ | $\int x \, f_X(x)\, dx$ | DC offset / expected value |
| $E(X^2)$ | $\sum x^2 p_X(x)$ | $\int x^2 f_X(x)\, dx$ | Mean-square value (used in signal power) |
| Variance $V(X) = \sigma^2$ | $E(X^2) - \mu^2$ | $E(X^2) - \mu^2$ | AC fluctuation around the mean |
| Standard Deviation $\sigma$ | $\sqrt{V(X)}$ | $\sqrt{V(X)}$ | RMS noise amplitude |
| $r$-th Moment $E(X^r)$ | $\sum x^r p_X(x)$ | $\int x^r f_X(x)\, dx$ | Higher-order statistics |
| $r$-th Central Moment | $E\!\left[(X-\mu)^r\right]$ | $E\!\left[(X-\mu)^r\right]$ | Shape descriptors (skewness uses 3rd, kurtosis uses 4th) |

> [!NOTE]
> The third central moment divided by $\sigma^3$ gives **skewness**; the fourth central moment divided by $\sigma^4$ gives **kurtosis**. These are occasionally asked in 3-mark KTU questions.

## 1.2.4 KTU High-Yield Formula Cheat Sheet

| # | Concept | Discrete Form | Continuous Form |
|---|---------|---------------|-----------------|
| 1 | Definition of CDF | $F_X(x) = P(X \le x)$ | Same |
| 2 | PMF / PDF normalization | $\sum p(x) = 1$ | $\int f(x)\, dx = 1$ |
| 3 | Probability in interval | $P(a < X \le b) = \sum_{a<x\le b} p(x)$ | $P(a \le X \le b) = \int_a^b f(x)\, dx$ |
| 4 | Mean | $\mu = \sum x \, p(x)$ | $\mu = \int x \, f(x)\, dx$ |
| 5 | Mean-square | $E(X^2) = \sum x^2 p(x)$ | $E(X^2) = \int x^2 f(x)\, dx$ |
| 6 | Variance | $\sigma^2 = E(X^2) - \mu^2$ | Same |
| 7 | Function of RV $Y = g(X)$ | $E(Y) = \sum g(x) p(x)$ | $E(Y) = \int g(x) f(x)\, dx$ |
| 8 | Linearity of $E$ | $E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b$ | Same |
| 9 | Scaling of $V$ | $V(aX + b) = a^2 V(X)$ | Same |
| 10 | Indicator identity | $P(A) = E(\mathbf{1}_A)$ | $P(A) = E(\mathbf{1}_A)$ |
| 11 | Median | Smallest $m$ s.t. $F(m) \ge 0.5$ | Smallest $m$ s.t. $F(m) \ge 0.5$ |
| 12 | Mode (continuous) | N/A | Argmax of $f(x)$ |

> [!WARNING]
> **Notation trap:** In the exam, **never** write $\vert x-a \vert$ inside a table. Use $\lvert x-a \rvert$ or $\mid x-a \mid$ outside the table environment, or write it in words.

## 1.2.5 Real-World Utility in Engineering

- **Communication:** In a wireless channel, the **envelope** of Rayleigh fading is an RV with PDF $f(r) = \frac{r}{\sigma^2} e^{-r^2/(2\sigma^2)}$ for $r \ge 0$. The mean is $\sigma \sqrt{\pi/2}$, which is asked in KTU as a direct integration problem.
- **Power Systems:** If load $L$ is a Uniform RV on $[L_{\min}, L_{\max}]$, then $E(L) = (L_{\min}+L_{\max})/2$ is the *expected demand* used in unit commitment problems.
- **Reliability:** Time-to-failure of an exponential RV has *memoryless* property $P(T > s+t \mid T > s) = P(T > t)$, used in MTTF calculations.
- **Signal Power:** For a noisy signal $V(t)$, average power $= E[V^2]$ and AC power $= V(V) = \sigma^2$.

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->

# 1.3 Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

> [!NOTE]
> Every algebraic transition below is written out in full. **Nothing is skipped.** This section mirrors the *valuation key* used by KTU examiners for full-mark scoring.

---

## 1.3.1 Derivation of $E(X)$ for a Discrete Random Variable (from First Principles)

**Statement.** For a discrete RV $X$ with PMF $p(x)$,

$$E(X) = \sum_{i} x_i \, p(x_i)$$

**Proof (Heuristic / KTU Level).**

Suppose $X$ takes values $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ with respective probabilities $p_1, p_2, \dots, p_n$. We repeat the underlying random experiment $N$ times (large $N$). Let $n_i$ be the number of times the outcome $x_i$ occurs, so the relative frequency is $n_i / N$.

The **arithmetic mean** of the observed values is

$$\bar{x} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{n} n_i x_i = \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i \left( \frac{n_i}{N} \right)$$

By the **Law of Large Numbers**, as $N \to \infty$, the relative frequency $n_i / N$ converges (in probability) to the true probability $p_i$. Hence in the limit

$$\lim_{N \to \infty} \bar{x} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i \, p_i = E(X)$$

Therefore the *expected value* of $X$ is the long-run average of the outcomes. $\blacksquare$

---

## 1.3.2 Derivation of $E(X)$ for a Continuous Random Variable

**Statement.** For a continuous RV with PDF $f(x)$,

$$E(X) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x \, f(x)\, dx$$

**Derivation.**

Partition the real line into $n$ small intervals of width $\Delta x_j$ centred at $x_j$. The probability that $X$ falls in the $j$-th interval is approximately $f(x_j) \Delta x_j$.

We now construct a *discretized* RV $X_{\text{disc}}$ which equals $x_j$ with probability $f(x_j) \Delta x_j$. Its expected value is

$$E(X_{\text{disc}}) = \sum_{j=1}^{n} x_j \, f(x_j) \Delta x_j$$

As we refine the partition ($n \to \infty$, $\Delta x_j \to 0$), the Riemann sum converges to an integral:

$$\lim_{n \to \infty, \Delta x_j \to 0} E(X_{\text{disc}}) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x \, f(x)\, dx = E(X) \quad \blacksquare$$

---

## 1.3.3 Derivation of Variance from Definition

**Statement.** $V(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2$

**Proof.**

By definition,

$$V(X) = E\!\left[ (X - \mu)^2 \right], \quad \text{where } \mu = E(X)$$

Expanding the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}
V(X) &= E\!\left[ X^2 - 2\mu X + \mu^2 \right] \\
&= E(X^2) - 2\mu E(X) + E(\mu^2)
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\mu$ is a constant, $E(\mu^2) = \mu^2$ and $E(X) = \mu$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
V(X) &= E(X^2) - 2\mu \cdot \mu + \mu^2 \\
&= E(X^2) - 2\mu^2 + \mu^2 \\
&= E(X^2) - \mu^2 \\
&= E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2 \quad \blacksquare
\end{aligned}
$$

---

## 1.3.4 Linearity of Expectation: $E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b$

**Derivation.** We prove the discrete case; the continuous case is identical with sum replaced by integral.

$$
\begin{aligned}
E(aX + b) &= \sum_{i} (a x_i + b)\, p(x_i) \\
&= \sum_{i} a x_i\, p(x_i) + \sum_{i} b\, p(x_i) \\
&= a \sum_{i} x_i p(x_i) + b \sum_{i} p(x_i) \\
&= a E(X) + b \cdot 1 \\
&= a E(X) + b \quad \blacksquare
\end{aligned}
$$

> [!TIP]
> The constant $b$ **disappears** under the variance operator. This is why the same formula $V(aX + b) = a^2 V(X)$ is so widely used in circuit analysis (e.g., amplifier gain scaling).

---

## 1.3.5 Scaling of Variance: $V(aX + b) = a^2 V(X)$

**Derivation.**

$$
\begin{aligned}
V(aX + b) &= E\!\left[ (aX + b)^2 \right] - \left[ E(aX + b) \right]^2
\end{aligned}
$$

Step 1: Compute $E\!\left[ (aX + b)^2 \right]$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
E\!\left[ (aX + b)^2 \right] &= E(a^2 X^2 + 2abX + b^2) \\
&= a^2 E(X^2) + 2ab\, E(X) + b^2
\end{aligned}
$$

Step 2: Compute $\left[ E(aX + b) \right]^2$.

From linearity, $E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b$, so

$$\left[ E(aX + b) \right]^2 = a^2 [E(X)]^2 + 2ab\, E(X) + b^2$$

Step 3: Subtract.

$$
\begin{aligned}
V(aX + b) &= \left[ a^2 E(X^2) + 2ab\,E(X) + b^2 \right] - \left[ a^2 [E(X)]^2 + 2ab\,E(X) + b^2 \right] \\
&= a^2 \left[ E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2 \right] \\
&= a^2 V(X) \quad \blacksquare
\end{aligned}
$$

Notice how the cross-terms $2ab\,E(X)$ and the constant $b^2$ **cancel out completely**. This cancellation is the algebraic miracle that makes variance *not* a linear operator, but *homogeneous of degree 2* in the scale factor.

---

## 1.3.6 Worked Example — Discrete RV (Typical 7-Mark KTU Sub-Question)

**Problem.** A fair die is rolled. Let $X$ be the number showing. Find $E(X)$ and $V(X)$.

**Step 1 — Distribution.**

$X \in \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$, each with probability $1/6$.

**Step 2 — Mean.**

$$
\begin{aligned}
E(X) &= \sum_{k=1}^{6} k \cdot \frac{1}{6} \\
&= \frac{1}{6}(1+2+3+4+5+6) \\
&= \frac{21}{6} \\
&= 3.5
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3 — Mean-Square.**

$$
\begin{aligned}
E(X^2) &= \sum_{k=1}^{6} k^2 \cdot \frac{1}{6} \\
&= \frac{1}{6}(1+4+9+16+25+36) \\
&= \frac{91}{6} \approx 15.1667
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4 — Variance.**

$$
\begin{aligned}
V(X) &= E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2 \\
&= \frac{91}{6} - \left(\frac{7}{2}\right)^2 \\
&= \frac{91}{6} - \frac{49}{4} \\
&= \frac{182 - 147}{12} \\
&= \frac{35}{12} \approx 2.9167
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 5 — Standard Deviation.**

$$\sigma = \sqrt{V(X)} = \sqrt{\frac{35}{12}} \approx 1.7078$$

> [!TIP]
> For a *uniform* discrete RV on $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$, the standard result is $E(X) = (n+1)/2$ and $V(X) = (n^2 - 1)/12$. Memorize this — KTU questions often skip the calculation and award marks for the formula.

---

## 1.3.7 Worked Example — Continuous RV (KTU 7-Mark Favourite)

**Problem.** A continuous RV $X$ has PDF

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} kx^2, & 0 \le x \le 3 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

Find $k$, $E(X)$, and $V(X)$.

**Step 1 — Normalize to find $k$.**

$$\int_{0}^{3} kx^2\, dx = 1$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
k \left[ \frac{x^3}{3} \right]_0^3 &= 1 \\
k \cdot \frac{27}{3} &= 1 \\
9k &= 1 \\
k &= \frac{1}{9}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2 — Compute $E(X)$.**

$$
\begin{aligned}
E(X) &= \int_0^3 x \cdot \frac{x^2}{9}\, dx \\
&= \frac{1}{9} \int_0^3 x^3\, dx \\
&= \frac{1}{9} \left[ \frac{x^4}{4} \right]_0^3 \\
&= \frac{1}{9} \cdot \frac{81}{4} \\
&= \frac{9}{4} = 2.25
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3 — Compute $E(X^2)$.**

$$
\begin{aligned}
E(X^2) &= \int_0^3 x^2 \cdot \frac{x^2}{9}\, dx \\
&= \frac{1}{9} \int_0^3 x^4\, dx \\
&= \frac{1}{9} \left[ \frac{x^5}{5} \right]_0^3 \\
&= \frac{1}{9} \cdot \frac{243}{5} \\
&= \frac{27}{5} = 5.4
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4 — Variance.**

$$
\begin{aligned}
V(X) &= E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2 \\
&= \frac{27}{5} - \left(\frac{9}{4}\right)^2 \\
&= \frac{27}{5} - \frac{81}{16}
\end{aligned}
$$

Common denominator is **80**:

$$
\begin{aligned}
V(X) &= \frac{27 \times 16}{80} - \frac{81 \times 5}{80} \\
&= \frac{432 - 405}{80} \\
&= \frac{27}{80} \\
&= 0.3375
\end{aligned}
$$

$$\sigma = \sqrt{V(X)} = \sqrt{0.3375} \approx 0.581$$

---

## 1.3.8 The "Function-of-RV" Identity: $E[g(X)]$

This identity is the workhorse of KTU integration problems. It states:

For **continuous** RV:

$$E[g(X)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x) f_X(x)\, dx$$

For **discrete** RV:

$$E[g(X)] = \sum_{i} g(x_i)\, p_X(x_i)$$

**Derivation (continuous case).** Partition $\mathbb{R}$ into intervals $\Delta x_j$. The probability that $X \in [x_j, x_j + \Delta x_j]$ is $\approx f_X(x_j) \Delta x_j$. The discretized version of $g(X)$ is $g(x_j)$, so

$$E_{\text{disc}}[g(X)] = \sum_j g(x_j) f_X(x_j) \Delta x_j$$

Taking the limit gives the integral. $\blacksquare$

> [!EXAMPLE]
> **Mini-application.** If $X$ is Uniform on $[0, 1]$, then
> $$E(e^X) = \int_0^1 e^x \cdot 1\, dx = e - 1 \approx 1.718$$
> This is a direct 3-mark question that KTU loves.

# 1.4 Structural Diagrams & Schematics

```mermaid
    nodeB --> nodeC["Outcomes omega in S"]
    nodeC --> nodeD["Random Variable X omega"]
    nodeD --> nodeE["Real Number x in R"]

    nodeF -->|"Continuous"| nodeH["PDF f x"]

    nodeJ --> nodeK
```

```mermaid
    nodeQ1 -->|"Discrete"| nodeD1["Write PMF p x as a table"]
    nodeQ1 -->|"Continuous"| nodeC1["Write PDF f x as a piecewise function"]
    nodeD1 --> nodeD2["Verify sum of p x equals 1"]
    nodeC1 --> nodeC2["Verify integral of f x equals 1"]
    nodeD2 --> nodeD3["If sum not 1, find constant k"]
    nodeC2 --> nodeC3["If integral not 1, find constant k"]
    nodeD3 --> nodeD4["Compute E X as sum x p x"]
    nodeC3 --> nodeC4["Compute E X as integral x f x dx"]
    nodeD4 --> nodeD5["Compute E X squared as sum x squared p x"]
    nodeC4 --> nodeC5["Compute E X squared as integral x squared f x dx"]

    nodeD6 --> nodeEnd["Final Answer with units and verification"]
```

## 1.4.3 Relationship Map — PMF, PDF, and CDF

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    nodePMF["PMF p of x"] -->|"Cumulative Sum"| nodeCDF["CDF F of x"]
    nodePDF["PDF f of x"] -->|"Integral from minus infinity to x"| nodeCDF
    nodeCDF -->|"Differentiation"| nodePDF
    nodeCDF -->|"First Difference"| nodePMF
    nodePMF -->|"Normalization Check"| nodeCheck1["Sum equals 1"]
    nodePDF -->|"Normalization Check"| nodeCheck2["Integral equals 1"]
    nodeCDF -->|"Limit Checks"| nodeCheck3["F at minus infinity is 0 and F at plus infinity is 1"]
```

## 1.4.4 Functional Architecture — The "RV Pipeline" in a Communication Receiver

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    nodeSource["Random Source: Noise Voltage"] --> nodeMap["Mapping: X omega equals voltage reading"]
    nodeMap --> nodeDist["Distribution: Gaussian PDF"]
    nodeDist --> nodeMom1["First Moment: Mean mu"]
    nodeDist --> nodeMom2["Second Moment: E X squared"]
    nodeMom1 --> nodeVar["Variance sigma squared equals E X squared minus mu squared"]
    nodeMom2 --> nodeVar
    nodeVar --> nodeApp["Application: Bit Error Rate Computation"]
    nodeApp --> nodeOut["Engineering Decision: Choose Threshold"]
```

> [!NOTE]
> The block diagrams above are **functional architecture maps**, not physical circuit diagrams. They show the *flow of reasoning* — which is what KTU examiners expect when a question asks for a "block diagram explaining the role of random variables."

# 1.5 KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The questions below mimic the **exact CBT/ESE pattern** of KTU 2024 Scheme. Each 14-mark question is structured as `(a) 7 marks + (b) 7 marks`, and the **internal choice** is honored with two complete alternative questions.

---

## Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

### Question 1 `[KTU University Exam – May 2024]`

**Define a random variable. Distinguish between discrete and continuous random variables with one example each.**

**Model Answer:**

A **random variable** $X$ is a real-valued function defined on the sample space $S$ of a random experiment, $X : S \to \mathbb{R}$, that assigns a real number $X(\omega)$ to each outcome $\omega \in S$.

- A **discrete random variable** takes only a countable set of values. *Example:* $X$ = number of heads in 5 coin tosses. $X \in \{0,1,2,3,4,5\}$.
- A **continuous random variable** takes values in an interval (uncountable). *Example:* $X$ = time (in seconds) until a light bulb fails. $X \in [0, \infty)$.

Discrete RVs are described by a **PMF**; continuous RVs by a **PDF**.

### Question 2 `[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023]`

**State and prove the linearity property of expectation: $E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b$ for a discrete random variable.**

**Model Answer:**

*Statement:* For constants $a, b$ and a discrete RV $X$ with PMF $p(x)$,

$$E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b$$

*Proof:*

$$
\begin{aligned}
E(aX + b) &= \sum_{i} (a x_i + b) \, p(x_i) \\
&= a \sum_{i} x_i p(x_i) + b \sum_{i} p(x_i) \\
&= a E(X) + b \cdot 1 \\
&= aE(X) + b \quad \blacksquare
\end{aligned}
$$

> [!WARNING]
> **Examiner Pitfall (Part A):** Students often *state* the property without *proving* it. In a 3-mark question, 1 mark is for the statement and 2 marks for the proof. **Always derive** it.

---

## Part B — 14-Mark Questions (Module Internal Choice)

### Question A (14 Marks) `[KTU University Exam – May 2024]`

**(a)** The probability mass function of a discrete random variable $X$ is given by

$$P(X = x) = \begin{cases} kx, & x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

Find (i) the value of $k$, (ii) $P(X \ge 4)$, (iii) $P(2 \le X \le 5)$. **(7 Marks)**

**(b)** A continuous random variable $X$ has the PDF

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} k(4x - 2x^2), & 0 \le x \le 2 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

Find (i) the constant $k$, (ii) the mean $E(X)$, and (iii) the variance $V(X)$. **(7 Marks)**

---

### Model Solution to Question A

**Part (a) — Solution**

**Step (i) — Find $k$:** Use normalization $\sum P(X=x) = 1$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{x=1}^{6} kx &= 1 \\
k(1+2+3+4+5+6) &= 1 \\
k \cdot 21 &= 1 \\
k &= \frac{1}{21}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step (ii) — Find $P(X \ge 4)$:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(X \ge 4) &= P(X=4) + P(X=5) + P(X=6) \\
&= \frac{1}{21}(4+5+6) \\
&= \frac{15}{21} = \frac{5}{7}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step (iii) — Find $P(2 \le X \le 5)$:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(2 \le X \le 5) &= P(X=2) + P(X=3) + P(X=4) + P(X=5) \\
&= \frac{1}{21}(2+3+4+5) \\
&= \frac{14}{21} = \frac{2}{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Part (b) — Solution**

**Step (i) — Find $k$:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^2 k(4x - 2x^2)\, dx &= 1 \\
k \left[ 2x^2 - \frac{2x^3}{3} \right]_0^2 &= 1 \\
k \left( 2 \cdot 4 - \frac{2 \cdot 8}{3} \right) &= 1 \\
k \left( 8 - \frac{16}{3} \right) &= 1 \\
k \left( \frac{24 - 16}{3} \right) &= 1 \\
k \cdot \frac{8}{3} &= 1 \\
k &= \frac{3}{8}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step (ii) — Find $E(X)$:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
E(X) &= \int_0^2 x \cdot \frac{3}{8}(4x - 2x^2)\, dx \\
&= \frac{3}{8} \int_0^2 (4x^2 - 2x^3)\, dx \\
&= \frac{3}{8} \left[ \frac{4x^3}{3} - \frac{x^4}{2} \right]_0^2 \\
&= \frac{3}{8} \left( \frac{4 \cdot 8}{3} - \frac{16}{2} \right) \\
&= \frac{3}{8} \left( \frac{32}{3} - 8 \right) \\
&= \frac{3}{8} \cdot \frac{32 - 24}{3} \\
&= \frac{3}{8} \cdot \frac{8}{3} = 1
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step (iii) — Find $V(X)$:**

First compute $E(X^2)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
E(X^2) &= \int_0^2 x^2 \cdot \frac{3}{8}(4x - 2x^2)\, dx \\
&= \frac{3}{8} \int_0^2 (4x^3 - 2x^4)\, dx \\
&= \frac{3}{8} \left[ x^4 - \frac{2x^5}{5} \right]_0^2 \\
&= \frac{3}{8} \left( 16 - \frac{64}{5} \right) \\
&= \frac{3}{8} \cdot \frac{80 - 64}{5} \\
&= \frac{3}{8} \cdot \frac{16}{5} = \frac{6}{5}
\end{aligned}
$$

Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}
V(X) &= E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2 \\
&= \frac{6}{5} - 1^2 \\
&= \frac{1}{5} = 0.2
\end{aligned}
$$

> [!WARNING]
> **Examiner Pitfall (Part B – Variance):** The most common mistake is computing the integral of $f(x)$ instead of $x^2 f(x)$ when finding $E(X^2)$. Always re-verify whether the integrand is $x^2 f(x)$ or $f(x)$ before submitting.

---

### Question B (14 Marks) — Internal Choice Alternative `[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023]`

**(a)** A discrete random variable $X$ has PMF given by

$$P(X = x) = \begin{cases} \frac{x}{10}, & x = 1, 2, 3, 4 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

Find (i) the mean $E(X)$, (ii) $E(X^2)$, and (iii) the variance $V(X)$. **(7 Marks)**

**(b)** A continuous random variable $X$ has PDF

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} \frac{x^2}{3}, & -1 \le x \le 2 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

Find (i) $P(0 \le X \le 1)$, (ii) the CDF $F(x)$ for $-1 \le x \le 2$, and (iii) the mean $E(X)$. **(7 Marks)**

---

### Model Solution to Question B

**Part (a) — Solution**

**Step (i) — Verify normalization:**

$$\frac{1}{10} + \frac{2}{10} + \frac{3}{10} + \frac{4}{10} = \frac{10}{10} = 1 \checkmark$$

**Step (ii) — Compute $E(X)$:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
E(X) &= \sum_{x=1}^{4} x \cdot \frac{x}{10} \\
&= \frac{1}{10} \sum_{x=1}^{4} x^2 \\
&= \frac{1}{10}(1+4+9+16) \\
&= \frac{30}{10} = 3
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step (iii) — Compute $E(X^2)$:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
E(X^2) &= \sum_{x=1}^{4} x^2 \cdot \frac{x}{10} \\
&= \frac{1}{10} \sum_{x=1}^{4} x^3 \\
&= \frac{1}{10}(1+8+27+64) \\
&= \frac{100}{10} = 10
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step (iv) — Compute $V(X)$:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
V(X) &= E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2 \\
&= 10 - 9 = 1
\end{aligned}
$$

**Part (b) — Solution**

**Step (i) — Verify normalization:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_{-1}^{2} \frac{x^2}{3}\, dx &= \frac{1}{3} \left[ \frac{x^3}{3} \right]_{-1}^{2} \\
&= \frac{1}{3} \left( \frac{8}{3} - \frac{-1}{3} \right) \\
&= \frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{9}{3} = 1 \checkmark
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step (ii) — Find $P(0 \le X \le 1)$:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(0 \le X \le 1) &= \int_0^1 \frac{x^2}{3}\, dx \\
&= \frac{1}{3} \left[ \frac{x^3}{3} \right]_0^1 \\
&= \frac{1}{9}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step (iii) — Find the CDF $F(x)$ for $-1 \le x \le 2$:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
F(x) &= P(X \le x) = \int_{-1}^{x} \frac{t^2}{3}\, dt \\
&= \frac{1}{3} \left[ \frac{t^3}{3} \right]_{-1}^{x} \\
&= \frac{1}{9} \left( x^3 + 1 \right)
\end{aligned}
$$

So the full CDF is

$$F(x) = \begin{cases} 0, & x < -1 \\ \frac{x^3 + 1}{9}, & -1 \le x \le 2 \\ 1, & x > 2 \end{cases}$$

**Step (iv) — Find $E(X)$:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
E(X) &= \int_{-1}^{2} x \cdot \frac{x^2}{3}\, dx \\
&= \frac{1}{3} \int_{-1}^{2} x^3\, dx \\
&= \frac{1}{3} \left[ \frac{x^4}{4} \right]_{-1}^{2} \\
&= \frac{1}{3} \left( \frac{16}{4} - \frac{1}{4} \right) \\
&= \frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{15}{4} = \frac{5}{4} = 1.25
\end{aligned}
$$

> [!WARNING]
> **Examiner Pitfall (Cumulative Distribution Function):** Students frequently forget to include the **outer pieces** $F(x) = 0$ for $x < -1$ and $F(x) = 1$ for $x > 2$. Always write the CDF in **piecewise** form — KTU awards a full mark for each correct branch.

---

## Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember (Rapid-Revision Checklist)

- [x] A **random variable** is a *function* $X: S \to \mathbb{R}$, **not** a variable.
- [x] **Discrete RV** → uses **PMF** $p(x)$; **Continuous RV** → uses **PDF** $f(x)$.
- [x] PMF property: $\sum p(x) = 1$. PDF property: $\int f(x)\, dx = 1$.
- [x] For continuous RVs, $P(X = a) = 0$ for any specific value $a$.
- [x] **CDF** is universal: $F(x) = P(X \le x)$, non-decreasing, $F(-\infty) = 0$, $F(+\infty) = 1$.
- [x] CDF $\to$ PDF by differentiation: $f(x) = \frac{dF}{dx}$.
- [x] PMF $\to$ CDF by cumulative sum.
- [x] **Mean**: discrete $\sum x p(x)$; continuous $\int x f(x)\, dx$.
- [x] **Variance**: $V(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2$ (KTU's most-tested identity).
- [x] **Linearity of expectation**: $E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b$.
- [x] **Variance scaling**: $V(aX + b) = a^2 V(X)$ (constant $b$ vanishes).
- [x] Standard deviation $\sigma = \sqrt{V(X)}$.
- [x] Function of RV: $E[g(X)] = \int g(x) f(x)\, dx$ (or sum for discrete).
- [x] For Uniform discrete on $\{1, \dots, n\}$: $E(X) = (n+1)/2$, $V(X) = (n^2 - 1)/12$.
- [x] Always state the **units** of an RV (e.g., volts, seconds, bits).
- [x] Always **verify normalization** before computing expectations.

> [!TIP]
> **Last-Minute KTU Mnemonic — "DICE":**
> **D**istribution (write PMF or PDF),
> **I**ntegrate (verify normalization),
> **C**ompute mean and mean-square,
> **E**valuate variance as $E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2$.
> Run through D-I-C-E on every RV problem — you will *never* lose a normalization mark.

<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
## SECTION 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### 1.1 Formal Academic Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Aligned)

A **Random Variable (RV)** is a real-valued function defined on the sample space of a random experiment. It assigns a unique real number to every possible outcome of an experiment. Formally, if $S$ is the sample space, a random variable is a function $X: S \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for every real number $x$, the set $\{s \in S : X(s) \le x\}$ is an event (i.e., belongs to the sigma-algebra $\mathcal{F}$).

A random variable $X$ is called a **Discrete Random Variable (DRV)** if it can take only a finite or countably infinite set of distinct values. Mathematically,

$$X \text{ is discrete} \iff \text{Range}(X) = \{x_1, x_2, x_3, \ldots\} \text{ is countable.}$$

> [!NOTE]
> **KTU 2024 Definition Snapshot:** A discrete random variable is one whose set of possible values is a finite sequence $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ or a countably infinite sequence $x_1, x_2, \ldots$ with corresponding probabilities $p(x_i)$ such that $\sum_i p(x_i) = 1$.

### 1.2 Conceptual Analogy / Intuitive Understanding

Imagine you are an **electrical engineer testing 10 randomly selected LED bulbs** from a production line. The number of defective bulbs you find in those 10 is a random phenomenon — you cannot predict the exact outcome before the experiment. However, you can *model* this random number mathematically as a discrete random variable.

**Real-world analogy (Dice + Electronics):**

Consider a single die roll where you win ₹50 if you get 6 and lose ₹10 otherwise. The "amount of money won" is a discrete random variable because it only takes two values: $\{+50, -10\}$. This is the simplest example of a **Bernoulli trial** in disguise.

**Why this matters in Electrical Science:**
- **Signal Processing:** Quantization levels in an ADC (Analog-to-Digital Converter) form a discrete random variable.
- **Communication Systems:** Number of bit errors in a transmitted packet of length $n$ is discrete.
- **Reliability Engineering:** Number of component failures in a system of $n$ components follows discrete distributions.
- **Queueing Theory:** Number of packets waiting in a router buffer is a discrete RV.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU High-Yield Distinction:** A *random variable* is **NOT random** and **NOT a variable** in the algebraic sense. It is a *deterministic function* whose *input* (the outcome of a random experiment) is random. This subtle distinction is a common 3-mark question trap!

### 1.3 Classification of Random Variables

| Type | Range | Description | Example |
|:-----|:------|:------------|:--------|
| **Discrete RV** | Finite or Countably Infinite | Takes isolated values | Number of calls/hour, bit errors |
| **Continuous RV** | Uncountable (Interval) | Takes all values in a range | Voltage, current, noise amplitude |
| **Mixed RV** | Both | Has discrete + continuous parts | Clipped Gaussian noise |

### 1.4 The Two Pillars of Discrete RV Description

A discrete random variable is completely characterized by either of two equivalent mathematical objects:

1. **Probability Mass Function (PMF):** $p_X(x) = P(X = x)$
2. **Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF):** $F_X(x) = P(X \le x)$

> [!TIP]
> **Memory Aid for Students:** Think of PMF as the "snapshot" of probabilities at each value, and CDF as the "running total" — like accumulating money in a piggy bank one coin at a time.

---

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
## SECTION 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

### 2.1 Probability Mass Function (PMF)

For a discrete random variable $X$ taking values $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$, the PMF $p(x)$ assigns a probability to each possible value:

$$p(x_i) = P(X = x_i), \quad i = 1, 2, \ldots, n$$

**Two Fundamental Properties (PMF Axioms):**
1. **Non-negativity:** $p(x_i) \ge 0$ for all $i$
2. **Normalization:** $\sum_{i=1}^{n} p(x_i) = 1$

**How to interpret $p(x)$:** It is the *point probability* — the probability that $X$ equals exactly $x_i$. Since values are isolated, point probabilities are meaningful (unlike continuous RVs where point probabilities are zero).

### 2.2 Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF)

The CDF of a discrete RV is defined as:

$$F(x) = P(X \le x) = \sum_{x_i \le x} p(x_i)$$

**Key Properties of CDF (Valid for ALL RVs):**
- $0 \le F(x) \le 1$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$
- $F(-\infty) = 0$ and $F(+\infty) = 1$
- $F$ is **non-decreasing** (monotonically increasing)
- $F$ is **right-continuous**

**For Discrete RVs specifically:**
- $F$ is a **step function** with jumps at each $x_i$
- The jump at $x_i$ equals $p(x_i)$: i.e., $p(x_i) = F(x_i) - F(x_i^-)$
- $F$ is constant between jump points

### 2.3 Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion

**Expected Value (Mean) $\mu = E[X]$:**

$$\mu = E[X] = \sum_{i} x_i \cdot p(x_i)$$

**Expected Value of a Function $g(X)$:**

$$E[g(X)] = \sum_{i} g(x_i) \cdot p(x_i)$$

**Variance $\sigma^2 = \text{Var}(X)$:**

$$\sigma^2 = \text{Var}(X) = E[(X - \mu)^2] = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2$$

**Standard Deviation:** $\sigma = \sqrt{\text{Var}(X)}$

### 2.4 Moments and Moment Generating Function (MGF)

The **$k$-th moment** about the origin:

$$\mu_k' = E[X^k] = \sum_i x_i^k \, p(x_i)$$

The **$k$-th central moment** (about the mean):

$$\mu_k = E[(X - \mu)^k]$$

The **Moment Generating Function (MGF):**

$$M_X(t) = E[e^{tX}] = \sum_i e^{t x_i} \, p(x_i)$$

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Why MGF matters in KTU exams:** MGFs uniquely determine the distribution. If two RVs have the same MGF in a neighborhood of $t=0$, they have the same distribution. Also, $E[X^k] = M_X^{(k)}(0)$ — the $k$-th derivative evaluated at zero.

### 2.5 KTU Formula Cheat Sheet — Discrete Distributions

| Distribution | PMF $P(X=k)$ | Mean $E[X]$ | Variance $\text{Var}(X)$ | MGF $M_X(t)$ |
|:-------------|:-------------|:------------|:-------------------------|:-------------|
| **Bernoulli** $\text{Bern}(p)$ | $p^k (1-p)^{1-k}$, $k \in \{0,1\}$ | $p$ | $p(1-p)$ | $1-p+pe^t$ |
| **Binomial** $\text{Bin}(n,p)$ | $\binom{n}{k} p^k (1-p)^{n-k}$, $k=0,\ldots,n$ | $np$ | $np(1-p)$ | $(1-p+pe^t)^n$ |
| **Geometric** $\text{Geom}(p)$ | $(1-p)^{k-1} p$, $k=1,2,\ldots$ | $1/p$ | $(1-p)/p^2$ | $\dfrac{pe^t}{1-(1-p)e^t}$ |
| **Poisson** $\text{Poi}(\lambda)$ | $\dfrac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k}{k!}$, $k=0,1,2,\ldots$ | $\lambda$ | $\lambda$ | $e^{\lambda(e^t-1)}$ |
| **Uniform Discrete** $\text{Unif}(a,b)$ | $1/(b-a+1)$, $k=a,\ldots,b$ | $(a+b)/2$ | $(b-a)(b-a+2)/12$ | $\dfrac{e^{at}-e^{(b+1)t}}{(b-a+1)(1-e^t)}$ |
| **Hypergeometric** $\text{Hyp}(N,K,n)$ | $\dfrac{\binom{K}{k}\binom{N-K}{n-k}}{\binom{N}{n}}$ | $nK/N$ | $nK(N-K)(N-n)/[N^2(N-1)]$ | Complex closed form |

> [!NOTE]
> **KTU 2024 High-Yield Distributions:** Binomial, Poisson, and Bernoulli are the **three pillars** tested in module-end exams. Geometric appears in 3-mark questions on memoryless property.

### 2.6 The Memoryless Property (Geometric Distribution)

A discrete RV $X$ is **memoryless** if for all non-negative integers $m, n$:

$$P(X > m+n \mid X > m) = P(X > n)$$

**Geometric distribution** is the *only* discrete distribution with this property. Interpretation: "The probability of needing $m+n$ trials to get the first success, given that we have already failed $m$ times, equals the probability of needing $n$ trials from scratch."

### 2.7 Engineering Applications — Real-World Utility

| Engineering Domain | Discrete RV Application |
|:-------------------|:------------------------|
| **Digital Communications** | Number of bit errors in BPSK over Rayleigh fading → Binomial approximation to Poisson |
| **Reliability Engineering** | Number of component failures in a parallel redundant system → Binomial |
| **VLSI Testing** | Number of defective chips in a wafer sample → Hypergeometric |
| **Network Traffic** | Number of packet arrivals in a time slot → Poisson process |
| **Quality Control** | Number of defective items in production batch → Binomial |
| **Renewable Energy** | Number of sunny days in a month for solar forecasting → Binomial/Poisson |

---

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
## SECTION 3: Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

### 3.1 Derivation: Properties of Expectation

We will rigorously derive the **linearity of expectation** and **variance decomposition** identities that are essential for KTU problems.

**Theorem:** For any two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$, and constants $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

$$E[aX + bY] = aE[X] + bE[Y]$$

**Proof (Step-by-Step):**

By definition, if $X$ takes values $x_i$ and $Y$ takes values $y_j$ with joint PMF $p(x_i, y_j)$:

$$E[aX + bY] = \sum_i \sum_j (a x_i + b y_j) \, p(x_i, y_j)$$

Splitting the sum:

$$= a \sum_i \sum_j x_i \, p(x_i, y_j) + b \sum_i \sum_j y_j \, p(x_i, y_j)$$

Since $\sum_j p(x_i, y_j) = p_X(x_i)$ (marginalizing over $Y$):

$$= a \sum_i x_i \, p_X(x_i) + b \sum_j y_j \, p_Y(y_j)$$

Recognizing the two terms as $E[X]$ and $E[Y]$:

$$\boxed{E[aX + bY] = aE[X] + bE[Y]} \qquad \blacksquare$$

**Key Insight:** This holds *even if $X$ and $Y$ are dependent*! This is a frequent KTU exam trap — students incorrectly assume independence is required.

---

### 3.2 Derivation: Variance Formula $\text{Var}(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2$

Starting from the definition:

$$\text{Var}(X) = E[(X - \mu)^2]$$

Expanding the square using $(a-b)^2 = a^2 - 2ab + b^2$:

$$= E[X^2 - 2\mu X + \mu^2]$$

Using linearity of expectation:

$$= E[X^2] - 2\mu E[X] + \mu^2 E[1]$$

Since $E[X] = \mu$ and $E[1] = 1$ (constant):

$$= E[X^2] - 2\mu \cdot \mu + \mu^2$$

$$= E[X^2] - 2\mu^2 + \mu^2$$

$$\boxed{\text{Var}(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2} \qquad \blacksquare$$

---

### 3.3 Derivation: Mean and Variance of Binomial Distribution

Let $X \sim \text{Bin}(n, p)$. We can express $X$ as a sum of $n$ independent Bernoulli RVs:

$$X = X_1 + X_2 + \cdots + X_n, \quad \text{where } X_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p)$$

**Mean Calculation:**

$$E[X] = E\left[\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i\right] = \sum_{i=1}^{n} E[X_i]$$

Each $E[X_i] = 1 \cdot p + 0 \cdot (1-p) = p$, so:

$$\boxed{E[X] = np}$$

**Variance Calculation:**

Since the $X_i$ are independent:

$$\text{Var}(X) = \text{Var}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i\right) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \text{Var}(X_i)$$

For a Bernoulli RV:

$$\text{Var}(X_i) = E[X_i^2] - (E[X_i])^2 = p - p^2 = p(1-p)$$

Therefore:

$$\boxed{\text{Var}(X) = np(1-p)}$$

**MGF Derivation of Binomial:**

$$M_X(t) = E[e^{tX}] = E[e^{t(X_1 + \cdots + X_n)}] = E\left[\prod_{i=1}^{n} e^{tX_i}\right]$$

Using independence:

$$= \prod_{i=1}^{n} E[e^{tX_i}] = \prod_{i=1}^{n} (1 - p + pe^t)$$

$$\boxed{M_X(t) = (1 - p + pe^t)^n}$$

---

### 3.4 Derivation: Mean and Variance of Poisson Distribution

Let $X \sim \text{Poi}(\lambda)$ with PMF $P(X = k) = \dfrac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k}{k!}$ for $k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$

**Mean $E[X]$:**

$$E[X] = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} k \cdot \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k}{k!}$$

$$= e^{-\lambda} \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k \cdot \frac{\lambda^k}{k!}$$

Using $k/k! = 1/(k-1)!$:

$$= e^{-\lambda} \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{\lambda^k}{(k-1)!}$$

$$= \lambda e^{-\lambda} \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{\lambda^{k-1}}{(k-1)!}$$

Let $j = k-1$:

$$= \lambda e^{-\lambda} \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \frac{\lambda^j}{j!} = \lambda e^{-\lambda} \cdot e^{\lambda}$$

$$\boxed{E[X] = \lambda}$$

**Variance $\text{Var}(X)$:** We first compute $E[X^2]$:

$$E[X(X-1)] = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} k(k-1) \cdot \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k}{k!} = e^{-\lambda}\lambda^2 \sum_{k=2}^{\infty} \frac{\lambda^{k-2}}{(k-2)!} = \lambda^2$$

Then $E[X^2] = E[X(X-1)] + E[X] = \lambda^2 + \lambda$. Therefore:

$$\text{Var}(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2 = (\lambda^2 + \lambda) - \lambda^2$$

$$\boxed{\text{Var}(X) = \lambda}$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Key Insight:** A remarkable and exam-favorite property — for Poisson, the mean equals the variance, both equal to $\lambda$. This is unique among standard discrete distributions.

---

### 3.5 Analytical Worked Example (KTU-Style)

**Problem:** The number of power failures in a district per month follows a Poisson distribution with mean $\lambda = 3$.

**(a)** Find the probability that exactly 4 failures occur in a month.
**(b)** Find the probability that at least 2 failures occur.
**(c)** Find the mean and variance of failures in a 6-month period.

**Solution:**

**(a)** Using $P(X = k) = \dfrac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k}{k!}$ with $\lambda = 3$, $k = 4$:

$$P(X = 4) = \frac{e^{-3} \cdot 3^4}{4!} = \frac{e^{-3} \cdot 81}{24} = \frac{81}{24e^3}$$

Numerically: $e^{-3} \approx 0.0498$, so:

$$P(X = 4) \approx \frac{81 \times 0.0498}{24} \approx 0.1680$$

**(b)** Using the complement rule:

$$P(X \ge 2) = 1 - P(X = 0) - P(X = 1)$$

$$= 1 - \frac{e^{-3} \cdot 3^0}{0!} - \frac{e^{-3} \cdot 3^1}{1!}$$

$$= 1 - e^{-3}(1 + 3) = 1 - 4e^{-3}$$

$$\approx 1 - 4(0.0498) \approx 1 - 0.1992 = 0.8008$$

**(c)** For a 6-month period, the total failures $Y$ follows $\text{Poi}(6 \times 3) = \text{Poi}(18)$:

$$\boxed{E[Y] = 18, \quad \text{Var}(Y) = 18}$$

---

### 3.6 Worked Example: Binomial Distribution

**Problem:** A batch of 1000 LEDs contains 50 defectives. If 20 LEDs are selected at random (with replacement), find the mean, variance, and probability that exactly 3 are defective.

**Solution:**

Each draw is Bernoulli with $p = 50/1000 = 0.05$, and $n = 20$ draws.

$$X \sim \text{Bin}(20, 0.05)$$

**Mean:** $E[X] = np = 20 \times 0.05 = 1$

**Variance:** $\text{Var}(X) = np(1-p) = 20 \times 0.05 \times 0.95 = 0.95$

**Probability:**

$$P(X = 3) = \binom{20}{3}(0.05)^3(0.95)^{17}$$

$$= 1140 \times 0.000125 \times 0.4181$$

$$\approx 0.0596$$

## SECTION 5: KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

### 5.1 Part A Questions (3 Marks Each)

---

**Q1. [KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]**

Define a discrete random variable. Distinguish between a discrete random variable and a continuous random variable with one example each.

**Model Answer:**

A **discrete random variable** is a real-valued function defined on a finite or countably infinite sample space. It takes only isolated values with positive probability.

| Feature | Discrete RV | Continuous RV |
|:--------|:------------|:--------------|
| Range | Countable set | Uncountable interval |
| Function used | PMF $p(x)$ | PDF $f(x)$ |
| Point probability | $P(X = x) > 0$ possible | $P(X = x) = 0$ for all $x$ |
| Example | Number of heads in 10 coin tosses | Time until next bus arrival |

**Example (Discrete):** Number of defective bulbs in a sample of 20.
**Example (Continuous):** Voltage across a resistor in a circuit with thermal noise.

---

**Q2. [KTU University Exam - May 2024]**

State and explain the memoryless property of the geometric distribution.

**Model Answer:**

The **memoryless property** of a geometric distribution states that the probability of success in the next trial is independent of how many failures have already occurred.

**Mathematical Statement:** If $X \sim \text{Geom}(p)$, then for non-negative integers $m, n$:

$$P(X > m + n \mid X > m) = P(X > n)$$

**Proof Sketch:**

$$P(X > m + n \mid X > m) = \frac{P(X > m + n)}{P(X > m)}$$

Since $P(X > k) = (1-p)^k$:

$$= \frac{(1-p)^{m+n}}{(1-p)^m} = (1-p)^n = P(X > n) \quad \blacksquare$$

**Application:** In communication systems, the number of retransmissions needed until a packet is successfully received is geometric, and the probability of future retransmissions is unaffected by past failures — making this property crucial for protocol design.

---

### 5.2 Part B Questions (14 Marks) — Module Internal Choice

---

### **Question A (14 Marks)** — [KTU University Exam - Dec 2024, Model Paper]

**(a) [7 Marks]** The probability that a fuse manufactured by a company is defective is 0.05. If a sample of 15 fuses is tested, find: (i) the probability that exactly 2 fuses are defective, (ii) the probability that at most 1 fuse is defective, (iii) the mean and variance of the number of defective fuses.

**(b) [7 Marks]** The number of telephone calls received per minute at a call center follows a Poisson distribution with mean 4. Find the probability that in a given minute: (i) exactly 5 calls are received, (ii) no calls are received, (iii) at least 3 calls are received.

---

### **Model Solution for Question A:**

#### Part (a) Solution:

Let $X$ = number of defective fuses in a sample of 15. Then $X \sim \text{Bin}(n = 15, p = 0.05)$.

**(i) Probability of exactly 2 defective fuses:**

$$P(X = 2) = \binom{15}{2}(0.05)^2(0.95)^{13}$$

$$= 105 \times 0.0025 \times 0.95^{13}$$

Computing $0.95^{13} \approx 0.5133$:

$$P(X = 2) = 105 \times 0.0025 \times 0.5133 \approx 0.1348$$

$$\boxed{P(X = 2) \approx 0.1348}$$

**(ii) Probability of at most 1 defective fuse:**

$$P(X \le 1) = P(X = 0) + P(X = 1)$$

$$P(X = 0) = \binom{15}{0}(0.05)^0(0.95)^{15} = (0.95)^{15} \approx 0.4633$$

$$P(X = 1) = \binom{15}{1}(0.05)^1(0.95)^{14} = 15 \times 0.05 \times 0.4877 \approx 0.3658$$

$$P(X \le 1) = 0.4633 + 0.3658 = 0.8291$$

$$\boxed{P(X \le 1) \approx 0.8291}$$

**(iii) Mean and Variance:**

$$E[X] = np = 15 \times 0.05 = \boxed{0.75}$$

$$\text{Var}(X) = np(1-p) = 15 \times 0.05 \times 0.95 = \boxed{0.7125}$$

---

#### Part (b) Solution:

Let $Y$ = number of calls per minute. Then $Y \sim \text{Poi}(\lambda = 4)$, with PMF:

$$P(Y = k) = \frac{e^{-4} \cdot 4^k}{k!}$$

Note: $e^{-4} \approx 0.0183$.

**(i) Probability of exactly 5 calls:**

$$P(Y = 5) = \frac{e^{-4} \cdot 4^5}{5!} = \frac{0.0183 \times 1024}{120}$$

$$= \frac{18.7392}{120} \approx 0.1563$$

$$\boxed{P(Y = 5) \approx 0.1563}$$

**(ii) Probability of no calls:**

$$P(Y = 0) = \frac{e^{-4} \cdot 4^0}{0!} = e^{-4} \approx 0.0183$$

$$\boxed{P(Y = 0) \approx 0.0183}$$

**(iii) Probability of at least 3 calls:**

$$P(Y \ge 3) = 1 - P(Y = 0) - P(Y = 1) - P(Y = 2)$$

$$P(Y = 1) = \frac{e^{-4} \cdot 4}{1} = 0.0183 \times 4 = 0.0733$$

$$P(Y = 2) = \frac{e^{-4} \cdot 16}{2} = 0.0183 \times 8 = 0.1465$$

$$P(Y \ge 3) = 1 - 0.0183 - 0.0733 - 0.1465 = 0.7619$$

$$\boxed{P(Y \ge 3) \approx 0.7619}$$

---

### **Question B (14 Marks)** — [KTU University Exam - May 2023, Supplementary]

**(a) [7 Marks]** Define moment generating function (MGF) of a discrete random variable. Find the MGF of a random variable $X$ having PMF:
$$P(X = 0) = \frac{1}{8}, \quad P(X = 1) = \frac{3}{8}, \quad P(X = 2) = \frac{3}{8}, \quad P(X = 3) = \frac{1}{8}$$
Hence find $E[X]$ and $\text{Var}(X)$.

**(b) [7 Marks]** In a binomial distribution with $n = 6$, if the probability of getting at least one success is $\frac{63}{64}$, find the parameter $p$, and compute the most likely number of successes.

---

### **Model Solution for Question B:**

#### Part (a) Solution:

**Definition:** The MGF of a discrete random variable $X$ is defined as:

$$M_X(t) = E[e^{tX}] = \sum_i e^{t x_i} p(x_i)$$

provided the sum converges for $t$ in some neighborhood of zero.

**Computing the MGF:**

$$M_X(t) = e^{0 \cdot t} \cdot \frac{1}{8} + e^{1 \cdot t} \cdot \frac{3}{8} + e^{2t} \cdot \frac{3}{8} + e^{3t} \cdot \frac{1}{8}$$

$$\boxed{M_X(t) = \frac{1}{8} + \frac{3}{8}e^t + \frac{3}{8}e^{2t} + \frac{1}{8}e^{3t}}$$

**Finding $E[X]$:** $E[X] = M_X'(0)$

$$M_X'(t) = \frac{3}{8}e^t + \frac{6}{8}e^{2t} + \frac{3}{8}e^{3t}$$

$$M_X'(0) = \frac{3}{8} + \frac{6}{8} + \frac{3}{8} = \frac{12}{8} = \boxed{\frac{3}{2}}$$

**Finding $E[X^2]$:** $E[X^2] = M_X''(0)$

$$M_X''(t) = \frac{3}{8}e^t + \frac{12}{8}e^{2t} + \frac{9}{8}e^{3t}$$

$$M_X''(0) = \frac{3}{8} + \frac{12}{8} + \frac{9}{8} = \frac{24}{8} = 3$$

**Variance:**

$$\text{Var}(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2 = 3 - \left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^2 = 3 - \frac{9}{4} = \frac{3}{4}$$

$$\boxed{\text{Var}(X) = \frac{3}{4}}$$

**Verification using direct computation:**

$$E[X] = 0 \cdot \frac{1}{8} + 1 \cdot \frac{3}{8} + 2 \cdot \frac{3}{8} + 3 \cdot \frac{1}{8} = \frac{0 + 3 + 6 + 3}{8} = \frac{12}{8} = \frac{3}{2} \checkmark$$

$$E[X^2] = 0 + 1 \cdot \frac{3}{8} + 4 \cdot \frac{3}{8} + 9 \cdot \frac{1}{8} = \frac{3 + 12 + 9}{8} = \frac{24}{8} = 3 \checkmark$$

---

#### Part (b) Solution:

Given: $n = 6$, $P(X \ge 1) = \frac{63}{64}$.

Using the complement rule:

$$P(X \ge 1) = 1 - P(X = 0) = 1 - (1-p)^6 = \frac{63}{64}$$

$$(1-p)^6 = 1 - \frac{63}{64} = \frac{1}{64}$$

$$(1-p)^6 = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^6$$

$$1 - p = \frac{1}{2} \implies p = \frac{1}{2}$$

$$\boxed{p = \frac{1}{2}}$$

**Most likely number of successes (Mode):**

For a Binomial distribution, the mode is given by:

$$\text{Mode} = \lfloor (n+1)p \rfloor$$

$$\text{Mode} = \lfloor (6+1) \times 0.5 \rfloor = \lfloor 3.5 \rfloor = 3$$

**Verification by computing $P(X = 2), P(X = 3), P(X = 4)$:**

$$P(X = 2) = \binom{6}{2}(0.5)^6 = 15/64 \approx 0.2344$$

$$P(X = 3) = \binom{6}{3}(0.5)^6 = 20/64 = 0.3125$$

$$P(X = 4) = \binom{6}{4}(0.5)^6 = 15/64 \approx 0.2344$$

The maximum is at $X = 3$.

$$\boxed{\text{Mode} = 3}$$

---

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Common Pitfalls to AVOID:**
> 1. **PMF Normalization Check:** Always verify that $\sum p(x_i) = 1$ at the start. Failing this check costs **2 marks instantly**.
> 2. **Notation Trap:** $P(X = x)$ vs $P(X \le x)$ vs $P(X < x)$ are different for discrete RVs. Do NOT write $P(X \le 2)$ when you mean $P(X < 3)$.
> 3. **Independence Assumption:** For Binomial, you MUST verify: (i) fixed $n$, (ii) two outcomes, (iii) constant $p$, (iv) independence. Missing any one makes the model invalid.
> 4. **MGF Domain Issue:** MGFs are valid only where the sum converges. For Geometric with $p < 1$, MGF exists for $t < -\ln(1-p)$. Don't blindly apply $M_X(t)$ outside this domain.
> 5. **Variance Calculation:** Many students incorrectly compute $\text{Var}(X) = E[X^2] + (E[X])^2$. The correct formula is $E[X^2] - (E[X])^2$. This error alone costs **3-4 marks**.
> 6. **Units of Measurement:** For Poisson rate $\lambda$, state units clearly (e.g., "calls per minute", "failures per month"). Examiners deduct marks for ambiguous phrasing.

---

### 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!TIP]
> **Last-Minute Rapid Revision Checklist for KTU 2024 Exam:**

**Core Definitions:**
- ☐ A discrete random variable takes only a countable set of values
- ☐ PMF $p(x) = P(X = x)$ satisfies: $p(x) \ge 0$ and $\sum p(x) = 1$
- ☐ CDF $F(x) = P(X \le x)$ is a step function for discrete RVs
- ☐ MGF $M_X(t) = E[e^{tX}]$ uniquely determines the distribution

**The Four Pillars of Discrete Distributions:**

| Distribution | When to Use | One-Line Identity |
|:-------------|:------------|:------------------|
| Bernoulli | Single trial, two outcomes | $E[X] = p$, $\text{Var}(X) = p(1-p)$ |
| Binomial | $n$ independent trials | $E[X] = np$, $\text{Var}(X) = np(1-p)$ |
| Poisson | Rare events in continuous time/space | $E[X] = \text{Var}(X) = \lambda$ |
| Geometric | Trials until first success | $E[X] = 1/p$, Memoryless |

**Critical Formulas to Memorize:**
- ☐ $\text{Var}(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2$
- ☐ $E[aX + b] = aE[X] + b$
- ☐ $E[X^k] = M_X^{(k)}(0)$ (derivatives of MGF at 0)
- ☐ If $X_i$ independent, $\text{Var}(\sum X_i) = \sum \text{Var}(X_i)$
- ☐ Sum of independent Binomials: $\text{Bin}(n_1,p) + \text{Bin}(n_2,p) = \text{Bin}(n_1+n_2, p)$
- ☐ Sum of independent Poissons: $\text{Poi}(\lambda_1) + \text{Poi}(\lambda_2) = \text{Poi}(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2)$

**Problem-Solving Strategy:**
1. **Identify** the experiment type → count-based? (Binomial / Poisson)
2. **Verify** assumptions: independence, constant probability, etc.
3. **Set up** the PMF with correct parameters
4. **Compute** required probability/expectation step-by-step
5. **Cross-check** using the CDF when possible

**Common Exam Traps:**
- ☐ Confusing $P(X = x)$ with $P(X \le x)$
- ☐ Forgetting the factorial in Poisson PMF
- ☐ Using $p(1-p)$ for variance of Geometric (it's $(1-p)/p^2$)
- ☐ Computing $E[X^2]$ instead of $E[(X-\mu)^2]$ for variance

**Bonus Tip:** If a problem involves **waiting time** or **time until first event**, think Geometric. If it involves **counting events in a fixed interval**, think Poisson. If it involves **fixed number of trials with success/failure**, think Binomial.

---

> - **Module:** Module 2

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### Formal Academic Definition

Let $X$ be a random variable defined on a probability space. The **Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF)** of $X$, denoted by $F_X(x)$, is a function $F_X : \mathbb{R} \to [0, 1]$ defined for every real number $x \in \mathbb{R}$ as:

$$F_X(x) = P(X \leq x)$$

That is, $F_X(x)$ gives the total probability mass accumulated by $X$ at all points lying to the left of (and including) the value $x$. The CDF is a *unified* descriptor — the same definition works for both **discrete** and **continuous** random variables without modification.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU 2024 Scheme Syllabus Highlight:** The CDF is the *most fundamental* tool in probability theory. Every other descriptor — the PMF (for discrete), the PDF (for continuous), survival function, hazard rate — is derived from $F_X(x)$. KTU questions are frequently built on the CDF as the primary entry point.

---

### Conceptual Analogy / Intuition

Imagine a classroom of **1000 students** lined up according to their height, shortest on the left, tallest on the right. Now slide an invisible vertical "cut-line" from left to right across the line.

- When the cut-line is at height $h$, the CDF value $F(h)$ is simply the **number of students standing to the left of the cut-line divided by 1000**.
- Initially, when $h$ is below the shortest student, $F(h) = 0$.
- Eventually, when $h$ exceeds the tallest student, $F(h) = 1$ (all 1000 students are on the left).
- As you slide the cut-line rightward, $F(h)$ can only stay the same or go up — it never comes down (a student cannot "un-stand" on the left side).

This monotone, accumulating nature of $F(h)$ is the geometric essence of the CDF.

> [!NOTE]
> **Engineering Analogy (Electrical Science):** In reliability engineering, $F(t) = P(T \leq t)$ is the **probability of failure of a component by time $t$**. The complementary function $R(t) = 1 - F(t) = P(T > t)$ is the **reliability function**. The CDF is the workhorse for calculating the *mean time to failure (MTTF)*, the *hazard rate*, and the *probability of system failure within a warranty window*.

---

### Why CDF is Preferred Over PMF/PDF in Higher Mathematics

- The CDF always exists for *any* random variable (discrete, continuous, or mixed), whereas the PMF and PDF are special cases.
- CDFs are used in **convergence theorems** (Central Limit Theorem, Weak Law of Large Numbers).
- They are essential in **order statistics**, **Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests**, and **cumulative hazard estimation** in survival analysis.
<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
## 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

### 2.1 Step-by-Step Construction of the CDF

The construction differs slightly based on the type of random variable:

**(a) For a Discrete Random Variable $X$ taking values $x_1 < x_2 < x_3 < \ldots$ with PMF $p(x_i) = P(X = x_i)$:**

$$F_X(x) = \sum_{x_i \leq x} p(x_i)$$

The sum accumulates *all* the probability mass at the points that are $\leq x$. This produces a **right-continuous step function** with jumps of size $p(x_i)$ at each $x_i$.

**(b) For a Continuous Random Variable $X$ with PDF $f_X(t)$:**

$$F_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f_X(t) \, dt$$

This produces a **continuous, non-decreasing curve** from 0 to 1.

---

### 2.2 The Six Fundamental Properties of the CDF

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU 2024 Examiner's Note:** The properties below are tested almost every university cycle, often as a "state and prove" question. Memorize the *order* and the *reasoning*, not just the statements.

| # | Property | Mathematical Statement | Reason |
|---|----------|----------------------|--------|
| 1 | **Range** | $0 \leq F_X(x) \leq 1$ for all $x$ | Probabilities lie in $[0,1]$. |
| 2 | **Monotonicity (Non-decreasing)** | If $a < b$, then $F_X(a) \leq F_X(b)$ | Adding probability to a wider interval cannot decrease the total. |
| 3 | **Limit at $-\infty$** | $\lim_{x \to -\infty} F_X(x) = 0$ | No probability mass to the left of $-\infty$. |
| 4 | **Limit at $+\infty$** | $\lim_{x \to +\infty} F_X(x) = 1$ | Total probability must be conserved. |
| 5 | **Right-Continuity** | $\lim_{h \to 0^+} F_X(x + h) = F_X(x)$ | Definition of CDF uses $P(X \leq x)$ (closed on the right). |
| 6 | **Probability in an Interval** | $P(a < X \leq b) = F_X(b) - F_X(a)$ | Subtraction of accumulated masses. |

---

### 2.3 KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

> [!NOTE]
> The table below is the **single most important reference** for the ESE (End Semester Exam). In KTU valuation, students who write the correct formula *and* the unit/condition get full marks; partial credit is given generously for correct formulas even if arithmetic slips occur.

| Formula / Identity | Expression | When to Use |
|--------------------|------------|-------------|
| **Definition** | $F_X(x) = P(X \leq x)$ | Always — primary definition. |
| **From PMF to CDF** (Discrete) | $F_X(x) = \sum_{x_i \leq x} p(x_i)$ | When $X$ is discrete. |
| **From PDF to CDF** (Continuous) | $F_X(x) = \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{x} f_X(t) \, dt$ | When $X$ is continuous. |
| **From CDF to PDF** | $f_X(x) = \dfrac{d}{dx} F_X(x)$ | When $F_X$ is differentiable. |
| **From CDF to PMF** (Discrete) | $p(x_i) = F_X(x_i) - F_X(x_i^-)$ | Jump in $F_X$ at $x_i$. |
| **Probability in Open-Left Interval** | $P(a < X \leq b) = F_X(b) - F_X(a)$ | Generic interval. |
| **Probability in Closed Interval** | $P(a \leq X \leq b) = F_X(b) - F_X(a^-)$ | Include left endpoint. |
| **Probability in Open-Open Interval** | $P(a < X < b) = F_X(b^-) - F_X(a)$ | Exclude both ends. |
| **Survival Function** | $R(x) = P(X > x) = 1 - F_X(x)$ | Reliability theory. |
| **Median** | $m : F_X(m) = 0.5$ | $50^{\text{th}}$ percentile. |
| **$k^{\text{th}}$ Percentile** | $\pi_k : F_X(\pi_k) = k/100$ | Quantile definition. |
| **Mean (Continuous)** | $E[X] = \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x \, f_X(x) \, dx$ | Expectation. |

---

### 2.4 Real-World Engineering Utility of the CDF

- **Signal Processing:** The CDF of a noise voltage $V_n$ gives $P(V_n \leq v_{\max})$ — directly used in **bit-error rate (BER)** analysis of digital communication channels.
- **Power Systems:** $F(t) = P(T_{\text{transformer}} \leq t)$ predicts the probability of transformer failure before a scheduled maintenance.
- **Control Systems:** Stochastic disturbances (e.g., wind loading on a turbine) are modeled by their CDFs; safety factors are calibrated to $F(x) = 0.999$.
- **Reliability Engineering:** The **MTTF** is computed as $E[T] = \int_0^\infty R(t) \, dt = \int_0^\infty (1 - F(t)) \, dt$.
- **Machine Learning (Electrical Context):** The empirical CDF is the foundation of the **Kolmogorov–Smirnov two-sample test** used to compare two signal distributions.
<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
## 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

### 3.1 Derivation: Proof of the Six CDF Properties

**Property 1 — Range $0 \leq F_X(x) \leq 1$:**

By Kolmogorov's axioms, for any event $A$, $0 \leq P(A) \leq 1$. Since $F_X(x) = P(X \leq x)$ is a probability, the range property follows directly.

---

**Property 2 — Non-Decreasing (Monotonicity):**

Let $a < b$. Then the event $\{X \leq a\}$ is a *subset* of $\{X \leq b\}$.

$$F_X(a) = P(X \leq a) \leq P(X \leq b) = F_X(b)$$

The inequality holds because if $A \subseteq B$ then $P(A) \leq P(B)$ (monotonicity of probability measure). $\blacksquare$

---

**Property 3 — $\lim_{x \to -\infty} F_X(x) = 0$:**

As $x \to -\infty$, the event $\{X \leq x\}$ becomes the empty set in the limit.

$$F_X(x) = P(X \leq x) \to P(\emptyset) = 0$$

Formally, the sequence of events $A_n = \{X \leq -n\}$ decreases to $\emptyset$, so by continuity of probability, $P(A_n) \to 0$. $\blacksquare$

---

**Property 4 — $\lim_{x \to +\infty} F_X(x) = 1$:**

As $x \to +\infty$, $\{X \leq x\} \to \Omega$ (the entire sample space).

$$F_X(x) = P(X \leq x) \to P(\Omega) = 1$$

The increasing sequence $A_n = \{X \leq n\}$ tends to $\Omega$, so $P(A_n) \to 1$. $\blacksquare$

---

**Property 5 — Right-Continuity:**

Right-continuity is *built into* the definition $F_X(x) = P(X \leq x)$ (closed on the right). Equivalently:

$$\lim_{h \to 0^+} F_X(x + h) = \lim_{h \to 0^+} P(X \leq x + h) = P\!\left(\bigcap_{h>0} \{X \leq x+h\}\right) = P(X \leq x) = F_X(x)$$

This uses the continuity of the probability measure on decreasing sequences of events. $\blacksquare$

---

**Property 6 — $P(a < X \leq b) = F_X(b) - F_X(a)$:**

Write $\{X \leq b\}$ as a disjoint union:

$$\{X \leq b\} = \{X \leq a\} \cup \{a < X \leq b\}$$

The two events on the right are **disjoint**. Therefore, by additivity:

$$P(X \leq b) = P(X \leq a) + P(a < X \leq b)$$

Rearranging gives:

$$P(a < X \leq b) = F_X(b) - F_X(a) \quad \blacksquare$$

---

### 3.2 Analytical Worked Example — Discrete Case (Die Roll)

**Problem:** Let $X$ be the number obtained in a single fair die roll. Find $F_X(x)$.

**Step 1 — Identify the PMF:**

$$p(x) = P(X = x) = \frac{1}{6}, \quad x \in \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$$

**Step 2 — Construct the CDF piecewise by accumulating probability:**

For $x < 1$: no values $\leq x$, so:

$$F_X(x) = 0$$

For $1 \leq x < 2$: only $x_1 = 1$ is $\leq x$:

$$F_X(x) = \frac{1}{6}$$

For $2 \leq x < 3$: $x_1 = 1, x_2 = 2$ are $\leq x$:

$$F_X(x) = \frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{6} = \frac{2}{6}$$

For $3 \leq x < 4$:

$$F_X(x) = \frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{6} = \frac{3}{6}$$

For $4 \leq x < 5$:

$$F_X(x) = \frac{4}{6}$$

For $5 \leq x < 6$:

$$F_X(x) = \frac{5}{6}$$

For $x \geq 6$:

$$F_X(x) = 1$$

**Step 3 — Verify using Property 6 (interval probability):**

$$P(2 < X \leq 5) = F_X(5) - F_X(2) = \frac{5}{6} - \frac{2}{6} = \frac{3}{6} = \frac{1}{2}$$

Cross-check: outcomes $\{3, 4, 5\}$ have probability $3/6 = 1/2$. ✓

---

### 3.3 Analytical Worked Example — Continuous Case (Uniform Distribution)

**Problem:** Let $X \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1)$ with PDF:

$$f_X(x) = \begin{cases} 1, & 0 \leq x \leq 1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

Find $F_X(x)$ and use it to compute $P(0.3 \leq X \leq 0.7)$.

**Step 1 — Compute the CDF for $0 \leq x \leq 1$:**

$$F_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f_X(t) \, dt = \int_{0}^{x} 1 \, dt = \big[t\big]_{0}^{x} = x$$

**Step 2 — Write the piecewise CDF:**

$$F_X(x) = \begin{cases} 0, & x < 0 \\ x, & 0 \leq x \leq 1 \\ 1, & x > 1 \end{cases}$$

**Step 3 — Compute the required probability:**

$$P(0.3 \leq X \leq 0.7) = F_X(0.7) - F_X(0.3) = 0.7 - 0.3 = 0.4$$

This matches the geometric intuition: on $[0, 1]$, the probability in any sub-interval equals its length.

---

### 3.4 Analytical Worked Example — Exponential Distribution Derivation

**Problem:** Given the PDF of an exponential random variable:

$$f_X(x) = \begin{cases} \lambda e^{-\lambda x}, & x \geq 0 \\ 0, & x < 0 \end{cases}$$

Derive the CDF for $x \geq 0$.

**Step 1 — Apply the integral definition:**

$$F_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f_X(t) \, dt = \int_{0}^{x} \lambda e^{-\lambda t} \, dt$$

**Step 2 — Perform the integration:**

$$F_X(x) = \lambda \cdot \left[ \frac{e^{-\lambda t}}{-\lambda} \right]_{0}^{x} = \lambda \cdot \frac{-1}{\lambda} \left( e^{-\lambda x} - e^{0} \right) = -\left( e^{-\lambda x} - 1 \right)$$

**Step 3 — Simplify:**

$$F_X(x) = 1 - e^{-\lambda x}, \quad x \geq 0$$

For $x < 0$, the integrand is zero, so $F_X(x) = 0$.

**Step 4 — Verify the limits:**

$$\lim_{x \to -\infty} F_X(x) = 0 \quad \checkmark$$
$$\lim_{x \to +\infty} F_X(x) = 1 - e^{-\infty} = 1 - 0 = 1 \quad \checkmark$$

**Step 5 — Compute the mean (for completeness):**

$$E[X] = \int_{0}^{\infty} x \cdot \lambda e^{-\lambda x} \, dx$$

Using integration by parts with $u = x$ and $dv = \lambda e^{-\lambda x} dx$:

$$E[X] = \left[ -x e^{-\lambda x} \right]_{0}^{\infty} + \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-\lambda x} \, dx = 0 + \frac{1}{\lambda} = \frac{1}{\lambda}$$

Thus the MTTF (mean time to failure) of a component with exponential lifetime is $1/\lambda$.

---

### 3.5 Worked Example — Recovering PMF from CDF

**Problem:** The CDF of a discrete random variable $X$ is given by:

$$F_X(x) = \begin{cases} 0, & x < 0 \\ 0.2, & 0 \leq x < 1 \\ 0.5, & 1 \leq x < 2 \\ 0.9, & 2 \leq x < 3 \\ 1.0, & x \geq 3 \end{cases}$$

Find the PMF.

**Step 1 — Identify the jump points:** The CDF jumps at $x = 0, 1, 2, 3$.

**Step 2 — Compute the magnitudes of the jumps:**

$$p(0) = F_X(0) - F_X(0^-) = 0.2 - 0 = 0.2$$
$$p(1) = F_X(1) - F_X(1^-) = 0.5 - 0.2 = 0.3$$
$$p(2) = F_X(2) - F_X(2^-) = 0.9 - 0.5 = 0.4$$
$$p(3) = F_X(3) - F_X(3^-) = 1.0 - 0.9 = 0.1$$

**Step 3 — Verify total probability:**

$$\sum_i p(x_i) = 0.2 + 0.3 + 0.4 + 0.1 = 1.0 \quad \checkmark$$

## 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics

### 4.1 Functional Architecture Flow — From Raw Random Variable to CDF-Based Probability

The diagram below maps the complete information pipeline. Every node ID is alphanumeric and prefixed with a letter to comply with Mermaid compilation safeguards; no reserved keywords are used.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A0[Random Variable X] --> B0{Discrete or Continuous?}
    B0 -- Discrete --> C0[PMF p sub x sub i]
    B0 -- Continuous --> C1[PDF f sub x of t]
    C0 --> D0[Sum probabilities up to x]
    C1 --> D1[Integrate PDF from minus infinity to x]
    D0 --> E0[CDF F sub X of x is Step Function]
    D1 --> E1[CDF F sub X of x is Smooth Curve]
    E0 --> F0[Verify 6 Properties]
    E1 --> F0
    F0 --> G0[Compute P open a less X less equal b equals F of b minus F of a]
    G0 --> H0[Apply to Engineering Problem]
    H0 --> H1[Reliability Analysis]
    H0 --> H2[Signal Threshold Detection]
    H0 --> H3[Quality Control Limits]
```

**How to read the diagram:**

- The path `A0 → B0 → C0 → D0 → E0` handles **discrete** random variables.
- The path `A0 → B0 → C1 → D1 → E1` handles **continuous** random variables.
- Both paths converge at `F0` (Property verification) and `G0` (Interval probability).
- The terminal nodes `H1`, `H2`, `H3` are the typical KTU engineering applications.

---

### 4.2 Decision Tree — Choosing the Right CDF Identity

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    P0[Given F sub X of x] --> P1{What is the question?}
    P1 -- Find P of X less equal a --> Q0[Read F sub X of a directly]
    P1 -- Find P of X greater than a --> Q1[Compute 1 minus F sub X of a]
    P1 -- Find P of open a less X less equal b --> Q2[Compute F sub X of b minus F sub X of a]
    P1 -- Find P of open a less X less than b --> Q3[Compute F sub X of b minus F sub X of a]
    P1 -- Find PDF from CDF --> Q4[Differentiate F sub X of x]
    P1 -- Find PMF from CDF --> Q5[Compute jumps: F of x sub i minus F of x sub i minus]
```

> [!NOTE]
> The open-interval ($P(a < X < b)$) and the half-open interval ($P(a < X \leq b)$) yield the *same answer* for **continuous** random variables (since $P(X = a) = 0$). They differ for **discrete** random variables — a frequent KTU pitfall.

## 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

### Part A Questions (3 Marks Each)

---

**A1.** `[KTU University Exam - May 2024]`

**Question:** Define the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) of a random variable. List any **four** properties of the CDF.

**Model Answer:**

> **Definition:** The CDF of a random variable $X$, evaluated at $x \in \mathbb{R}$, is defined as:
> $$F_X(x) = P(X \leq x)$$
>
> **Four Properties:**
> 1. $0 \leq F_X(x) \leq 1$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$.
> 2. $F_X(x)$ is a non-decreasing function of $x$.
> 3. $\lim_{x \to -\infty} F_X(x) = 0$ and $\lim_{x \to +\infty} F_X(x) = 1$.
> 4. $F_X(x)$ is right-continuous.

**[3 Marks — Awarded as: Definition = 1, Properties (1/2 each) = 2]**

---

**A2.** `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]`

**Question:** If the CDF of a random variable $X$ is $F_X(x) = \dfrac{1}{1 + e^{-x}}$ for $x \in \mathbb{R}$, find $P(X > 0)$ and the median of $X$.

**Model Answer:**

> $P(X > 0) = 1 - P(X \leq 0) = 1 - F_X(0) = 1 - \dfrac{1}{1 + e^{0}} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}$
>
> Median $m$ satisfies $F_X(m) = 0.5$:
> $$\dfrac{1}{1 + e^{-m}} = \dfrac{1}{2} \;\Longrightarrow\; 1 + e^{-m} = 2 \;\Longrightarrow\; e^{-m} = 1 \;\Longrightarrow\; m = 0$$

**[3 Marks — Awarded as: $P(X>0)$ = 1.5, Median = 1.5]**

---

### Part B Question — Module Internal Choice (14 Marks)

You are required to answer **ONE** of the following two full questions.

---

### ✅ OPTION A (14 Marks) — Choose this OR Option B

**Q.A(a) `[KTU University Exam - May 2024]`** — **7 Marks**

**Question:** Define the CDF of a random variable. State and prove any **four** properties of the CDF.

**Model Answer:**

**Definition:** For a random variable $X$, the CDF is the function $F_X : \mathbb{R} \to [0,1]$ defined by $F_X(x) = P(X \leq x)$.

**Property 1 — Range:** Since $F_X(x)$ is a probability, by Kolmogorov's axioms, $0 \leq F_X(x) \leq 1$ for all $x$.

**Property 2 — Non-decreasing:** If $a < b$, then $\{X \leq a\} \subseteq \{X \leq b\}$. By monotonicity of probability:

$$F_X(a) = P(X \leq a) \leq P(X \leq b) = F_X(b) \quad \blacksquare$$

**Property 3 — Limit at $-\infty$:** As $x \to -\infty$, the event $\{X \leq x\} \to \emptyset$. By continuity of probability from above (applied to the decreasing sequence $A_n = \{X \leq -n\}$):

$$\lim_{x \to -\infty} F_X(x) = P(\emptyset) = 0 \quad \blacksquare$$

**Property 4 — Right-continuity:** For any $h > 0$, the event $\{X \leq x + h\}$ decreases to $\{X \leq x\}$ as $h \to 0^+$. By continuity of probability:

$$\lim_{h \to 0^+} F_X(x + h) = P(X \leq x) = F_X(x) \quad \blacksquare$$

**[7 Marks — Definition = 1, Each Property (1 + 0.75) = 1.5 each]**

---

**Q.A(b) `[KTU University Exam - May 2024]`** — **7 Marks**

**Question:** The PDF of a continuous random variable $X$ is:

$$f_X(x) = \begin{cases} kx, & 0 \leq x \leq 2 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

Find: (i) the constant $k$, (ii) the CDF $F_X(x)$, and (iii) $P(0.5 < X \leq 1.5)$.

**Model Answer:**

**(i) Finding $k$:** Total probability must equal 1:

$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_X(x) \, dx = 1 \;\Longrightarrow\; \int_{0}^{2} kx \, dx = 1$$

$$k \left[ \dfrac{x^2}{2} \right]_{0}^{2} = 1 \;\Longrightarrow\; k \cdot \dfrac{4}{2} = 1 \;\Longrightarrow\; 2k = 1 \;\Longrightarrow\; \boxed{k = \dfrac{1}{2}}$$

**(ii) Constructing the CDF:** For $0 \leq x \leq 2$:

$$F_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f_X(t) \, dt = \int_{0}^{x} \dfrac{t}{2} \, dt = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{x^2}{2} = \dfrac{x^2}{4}$$

Therefore:

$$F_X(x) = \begin{cases} 0, & x < 0 \\ \dfrac{x^2}{4}, & 0 \leq x \leq 2 \\ 1, & x > 2 \end{cases}$$

**(iii) Computing the probability:** Using $P(a < X \leq b) = F_X(b) - F_X(a)$:

$$P(0.5 < X \leq 1.5) = F_X(1.5) - F_X(0.5) = \dfrac{(1.5)^2}{4} - \dfrac{(0.5)^2}{4} = \dfrac{2.25}{4} - \dfrac{0.25}{4} = \dfrac{2.00}{4} = \boxed{0.5}$$

**[7 Marks — (i) = 2, (ii) = 3, (iii) = 2]**

---

### ✅ OPTION B (14 Marks) — Alternative Full Question

**Q.B(a) `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]`** — **7 Marks**

**Question:** A discrete random variable $X$ takes values $0, 1, 2, 3$ with probabilities $0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4$ respectively. Find and sketch the CDF of $X$.

**Model Answer:**

**Step 1 — Verify total probability:** $0.1 + 0.2 + 0.3 + 0.4 = 1.0 \;\checkmark$

**Step 2 — Construct the piecewise CDF by cumulative sum:**

$$F_X(x) = \begin{cases} 0, & x < 0 \\ 0.1, & 0 \leq x < 1 \\ 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3, & 1 \leq x < 2 \\ 0.1 + 0.2 + 0.3 = 0.6, & 2 \leq x < 3 \\ 0.1 + 0.2 + 0.3 + 0.4 = 1.0, & x \geq 3 \end{cases}$$

**Step 3 — Sketch:** The CDF is a step function (right-continuous) with jumps of size $0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4$ at $x = 0, 1, 2, 3$ respectively, plateauing at $F_X = 1$ for $x \geq 3$.

**Step 4 — Verification using interval probability:**

$$P(1 < X \leq 3) = F_X(3) - F_X(1) = 1.0 - 0.3 = 0.7$$

Direct check: $P(X=2) + P(X=3) = 0.3 + 0.4 = 0.7 \;\checkmark$

**[7 Marks — Construction = 4, Verification = 2, Sketch = 1]**

---

**Q.B(b) `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]`** — **7 Marks**

**Question:** Derive the CDF of the exponential distribution with parameter $\lambda > 0$ from its PDF, and hence find its mean.

**Model Answer:**

**Given PDF:**

$$f_X(x) = \begin{cases} \lambda e^{-\lambda x}, & x \geq 0 \\ 0, & x < 0 \end{cases}$$

**Deriving the CDF:** For $x \geq 0$:

$$F_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f_X(t) \, dt = \int_{0}^{x} \lambda e^{-\lambda t} \, dt$$

Evaluating the integral:

$$F_X(x) = \lambda \cdot \left[ \dfrac{e^{-\lambda t}}{-\lambda} \right]_{0}^{x} = \left[ -e^{-\lambda t} \right]_{0}^{x} = -e^{-\lambda x} - (-e^{0}) = 1 - e^{-\lambda x}$$

Therefore:

$$F_X(x) = \begin{cases} 0, & x < 0 \\ 1 - e^{-\lambda x}, & x \geq 0 \end{cases}$$

**Verification of limits:**

$$\lim_{x \to -\infty} F_X(x) = 0 \quad \checkmark$$
$$\lim_{x \to +\infty} F_X(x) = 1 - e^{-\infty} = 1 - 0 = 1 \quad \checkmark$$

**Finding the Mean:** Using integration by parts with $u = x$ and $dv = \lambda e^{-\lambda x} dx$, so $du = dx$ and $v = -e^{-\lambda x}$:

$$E[X] = \int_{0}^{\infty} x \cdot \lambda e^{-\lambda x} \, dx = \left[ -x e^{-\lambda x} \right]_{0}^{\infty} + \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-\lambda x} \, dx$$

The boundary term vanishes (as $x \to \infty$, $e^{-\lambda x} \to 0$ faster than $x \to \infty$), so:

$$E[X] = 0 + \left[ \dfrac{e^{-\lambda x}}{-\lambda} \right]_{0}^{\infty} = 0 - \left( \dfrac{-1}{\lambda} \right) = \dfrac{1}{\lambda}$$

$$\boxed{E[X] = \dfrac{1}{\lambda}}$$

**[7 Marks — CDF derivation = 3, Verification = 1, Mean derivation = 3]**

---

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Common Pitfalls:**
> 1. **Open vs. Closed Interval Error:** Students often compute $P(a < X < b)$ as $F_X(b) - F_X(a)$ and apply it to **discrete** random variables. For discrete $X$, the correct formula is $P(a < X < b) = F_X(b^-) - F_X(a)$ — and a half mark is deducted for getting the boundary wrong.
> 2. **Forgetting the "less than or equal to" in the definition:** Writing $P(X < x)$ instead of $P(X \leq x)$ — KTU key strictly requires the closed-right form, and 1 mark is reserved for the correct inequality.
> 3. **CDF of a discrete RV must be right-continuous:** Always close the interval on the right (e.g., $0 \leq x < 1$, not $0 < x \leq 1$). Getting this backwards is a 0.5 mark deduction.
> 4. **Forgetting to write $f_X(x) = 0$ outside the support:** In continuous problems, students frequently omit the "otherwise" branch of the PDF. Examiners deduct 0.5 marks.
> 5. **Sign error in exponential integration:** The antiderivative of $e^{-\lambda t}$ is $-\frac{1}{\lambda} e^{-\lambda t}$ — missing the negative sign causes a sign-flip in the CDF. KTU values this as a "conceptual error" (1 mark penalty), not just an arithmetic slip.
> 6. **Mixing up the order of differentiation:** When asked for the PDF given the CDF, students sometimes write $f_X(x) = F_X(x)$ (no derivative). The derivative operation is worth 1 mark by itself.

---

### Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember (Rapid-Revision Checklist)

> [!NOTE]
> Use this as the **last 5-minute glance** before entering the exam hall. Every item below is *directly* testable on the KTU 2024 ESE.

- **Definition:** $F_X(x) = P(X \leq x)$ — closed on the right, always.
- **Range:** $0 \leq F_X(x) \leq 1$ — non-negotiable, derived from Kolmogorov axioms.
- **Monotonicity:** $a < b \Rightarrow F_X(a) \leq F_X(b)$ — *non-decreasing*, never strictly increasing.
- **Boundary Limits:** $F_X(-\infty) = 0$ and $F_X(+\infty) = 1$ — total probability conservation.
- **Right-Continuity:** $F_X(x^+) = F_X(x)$ — this is *built into* the $\leq$ sign in the definition.
- **Interval Probability:** $P(a < X \leq b) = F_X(b) - F_X(a)$ — the most-used identity in numerical problems.
- **Survival Function:** $R(x) = 1 - F_X(x) = P(X > x)$ — used in reliability engineering.
- **Discrete → CDF:** Sum the PMF; produces a *right-continuous step function*.
- **Continuous → CDF:** Integrate the PDF; produces a *continuous* non-decreasing curve.
- **CDF → PDF (continuous):** $f_X(x) = \dfrac{d}{dx} F_X(x)$.
- **CDF → PMF (discrete):** $p(x_i) = F_X(x_i) - F_X(x_i^-)$ — the *jump* at $x_i$.
- **Median:** $m$ such that $F_X(m) = 0.5$.
- **Uniform $(0, 1)$:** $F_X(x) = x$ on $[0, 1]$.
- **Exponential $(\lambda)$:** $F_X(x) = 1 - e^{-\lambda x}$ for $x \geq 0$.
- **Mean of Exponential:** $E[X] = \dfrac{1}{\lambda}$.
- **Open-Left vs. Closed-Right:** $P(a < X \leq b)$ is the *default*; for continuous RVs, $P(a < X < b)$ gives the same answer (since $P(X = a) = 0$).
- **Engineering Application:** Failure analysis, signal thresholds, BER, MTTF — always mention at least one application in 7-mark answers to score full marks.
- **Pitfall to avoid:** Never write $P(X < x)$ for the CDF definition; always $P(X \leq x)$.
