> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME** > - **Course:** GBMAT401 - MATHEMATICS FOR ELECTRICAL SCIENCE – 4 > - **Module:** Module 2 > - **Topic:** Expected Value of a Function of Two Continuous Variables ## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview ### 1.1 Formal Academic Definition In the framework of probability theory for **two continuous random variables** $X$ and $Y$ defined over a sample space $\Omega$, the **Expected Value (Mathematical Expectation)** of a real-valued function $g(X, Y)$ — where $g : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ — is defined as the double integral of $g(x,y)$ weighted by the **joint probability density function** $f_{X,Y}(x, y)$ over the entire $\mathbb{R}^2$ plane. > [!IMPORTANT] > **KTU 2024 Syllabus Definition:** > If $X$ and $Y$ are two continuous random variables with joint probability density function (joint PDF) $f_{X,Y}(x,y)$, then the **expected value** of a function $g(X, Y)$ is given by: > $$E[g(X,Y)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x,y) \, f_{X,Y}(x,y) \, dx \, dy$$ > provided the integral converges absolutely, i.e., $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \vert g(x,y) \vert \, f_{X,Y}(x,y) \, dx \, dy < \infty$. ### 1.2 Conceptual Analogy — The "Weighted Average of an Infinite Mosaic" Imagine the $xy$-plane tiled with a **glowing density mosaic** where the brightness at every point $(x, y)$ is exactly $f_{X,Y}(x, y)$ — a density (not a probability) that integrates to **1** over the whole plane. Now place a **3D translucent sheet** above the plane whose height at every point is $g(x, y)$. The "expected value" is essentially the **center of mass** of the volume under the curved surface $g(x,y) \cdot f_{X,Y}(x,y)$ — projected onto the $z$-axis. In simpler words, it is the long-run *average* of $g(X,Y)$ if you sampled $(X, Y)$ infinitely many times and computed $g$ each time. > [!NOTE] > **Key Insight for KTU Students:** The expected value is *not* the most likely outcome (that would be the mode), nor the middle outcome (that would be the median). It is the **probability-weighted centroid** of the distribution. ### 1.3 Physical and Engineering Metrics - The dimension of $E[g(X,Y)]$ equals the dimension of $g$ itself (e.g., if $g(X,Y) = X^2 + Y^2$ and $X, Y$ are in **metres (m)**, then $E[g]$ is in **$\text{m}^2$**). - The joint PDF $f_{X,Y}(x,y)$ has units of **(unit of $X$)⁻¹ · (unit of $Y$)⁻¹** so that the double integral is **dimensionless** (since probability is dimensionless). > [!TIP] > **Always validate**: $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,y) \, dx \, dy = 1$. If this fails, your $f_{X,Y}$ is not a valid joint PDF. ## 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet ### 2.1 Foundational Logic of the Definition The expected value $E[g(X,Y)]$ is constructed by three conceptual steps: 1. **Discretization (Heuristic)**: Partition the $xy$-plane into infinitesimal rectangles of area $dx\,dy$. The probability that $(X,Y)$ falls in the small rectangle around $(x,y)$ is approximately $f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dx\,dy$. 2. **Weighting**: Multiply this small probability by the value $g(x,y)$. 3. **Aggregation (Integration)**: Sum (integrate) over all such rectangles to obtain the "average" outcome. Mathematically, the construction parallels the single-variable case where $E[g(X)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x) f_X(x)\,dx$. ### 2.2 Special Cases (Most Important for KTU) By substituting specific forms of $g(x,y)$, we recover the elementary moments: | Function $g(x,y)$ | Quantity | Formula | |---|---|---| | $g(x,y) = x$ | Mean of $X$ | $E[X] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x \, f_{X,Y}(x,y) \, dy\,dx$ | | $g(x,y) = y$ | Mean of $Y$ | $E[Y] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} y \, f_{X,Y}(x,y) \, dy\,dx$ | | $g(x,y) = x^2$ | Second moment of $X$ | $E[X^2] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x^2 \, f_{X,Y}(x,y) \, dy\,dx$ | | $g(x,y) = y^2$ | Second moment of $Y$ | $E[Y^2] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} y^2 \, f_{X,Y}(x,y) \, dy\,dx$ | | $g(x,y) = xy$ | Cross moment | $E[XY] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} xy \, f_{X,Y}(x,y) \, dy\,dx$ | | $g(x,y) = (x - \mu_X)(y - \mu_Y)$ | Covariance | $\text{Cov}(X,Y) = E[XY] - E[X]\,E[Y]$ | | $g(x,y) = ax + by + c$ | Linear combination | $E[aX + bY + c] = aE[X] + bE[Y] + c$ | > [!IMPORTANT] > **Why does the inner integral disappear in the marginal-moment case?** > Because $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dy = f_X(x)$ (the marginal PDF of $X$), we have: > $$E[X] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x \left[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dy\right] dx = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x \, f_X(x)\,dx$$ > This is the single-variable result, derived rigorously from the 2D definition. ### 2.3 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet | # | Formula Name | Mathematical Expression | Conditions / Notes | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | General Expectation of $g(X,Y)$ | $E[g(X,Y)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x,y)\,f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dx\,dy$ | Valid when integral converges absolutely | | 2 | Linearity of Expectation | $E[a\,g_1(X,Y) + b\,g_2(X,Y)] = a\,E[g_1(X,Y)] + b\,E[g_2(X,Y)]$ | $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ constants; **always valid** | | 3 | Linearity in Variables | $E[aX + bY + c] = aE[X] + bE[Y] + c$ | No independence required! | | 4 | Multiplicativity (Independence) | $E[g(X)h(Y)] = E[g(X)]\,E[h(Y)]$ | Only if $X$ and $Y$ are **independent**, i.e. $f_{X,Y} = f_X f_Y$ | | 5 | Variance Decomposition | $\text{Var}(aX + bY) = a^2\text{Var}(X) + b^2\text{Var}(Y) + 2ab\,\text{Cov}(X,Y)$ | Reduces if $X \perp Y$ (last term vanishes) | | 6 | Covariance Identity | $\text{Cov}(X,Y) = E[XY] - E[X]\,E[Y]$ | Used in nearly every KTU problem | | 7 | Correlation Coefficient | $\rho_{X,Y} = \dfrac{\text{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sqrt{\text{Var}(X)\,\text{Var}(Y)}}$ | $\rho \in [-1, +1]$; measures **linear dependence** | | 8 | Joint PDF Validity | $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dx\,dy = 1$ | $f_{X,Y}(x,y) \geq 0$ for all $(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2$ | | 9 | Marginal PDF | $f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dy$ | Symmetric formula for $f_Y(y)$ | | 10 | Conditional Expectation | $E[X \mid Y = y] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x\,f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)\,dx$ | A full random variable; the KTU sometimes tests this | ### 2.4 Real-World Engineering Utility - **Signal Processing**: $E[X^2]$ represents the **average power** of a stochastic signal $X(t)$ — a cornerstone of communication theory. - **Reliability Engineering**: $E[\max(X,Y)]$ models the **system lifetime** of parallel redundant components. - **Power Systems**: $E[VI]$ gives the **expected power delivery** in a noisy load circuit. - **Control Systems**: $\text{Cov}(X,Y)$ measures how two noisy sensor readings drift together; $\rho = 0$ implies uncorrelatedness (a precursor to Kalman filter design). - **Machine Learning / AI**: The **mean squared error** loss is precisely $E[(Y - \hat{Y})^2]$, decomposed into bias² + variance + noise. > [!TIP] > The KTU 2024 scheme frequently tests the difference between **independence** ($\Rightarrow$ uncorrelatedness) and **uncorrelatedness** ($\not\Rightarrow$ independence in general, though they coincide for jointly Gaussian random variables). ## 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix ### 3.1 Derivation: From the Single-Variable Definition to the Two-Variable Case **Step 1 — Recall the discrete one-variable expectation.** For a discrete random variable $X$ taking values $x_i$ with probabilities $p_i$: $$E[X] = \sum_{i} x_i \, p_i$$ **Step 2 — Extend to two discrete random variables.** For a function $g(X, Y)$ with joint PMF $P(X = x_i, Y = y_j) = p_{ij}$: $$E[g(X,Y)] = \sum_{i}\sum_{j} g(x_i, y_j) \, p_{ij}$$ **Step 3 — Pass to the continuous limit.** Replace the discrete sum with a double Riemann integral. The probability mass $p_{ij}$ over an infinitesimal rectangle of area $dx\,dy$ becomes the density $f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dx\,dy$: $$\sum_{i}\sum_{j} g(x_i, y_j) \, p_{ij} \;\longrightarrow\; \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x,y)\,f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dx\,dy$$ **Result:** $$E[g(X,Y)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x,y)\,f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dx\,dy \qquad \blacksquare$$ ### 3.2 Derivation: Linearity of Expectation for Two Variables **Claim:** $E[aX + bY + c] = aE[X] + bE[Y] + c$, where $a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}$ are constants. **Step 1 — Set $g(x,y) = ax + by + c$.** Substitute into the defining integral: $$E[aX + bY + c] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} (ax + by + c)\,f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dy\,dx$$ **Step 2 — Distribute the integrand** (integral is linear): $$E[aX + bY + c] = a\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x\,f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dy\,dx + b\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} y\,f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dy\,dx + c\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dy\,dx$$ **Step 3 — Identify each piece.** By the marginal-PDF relation (Formula 9 above), the inner integrals reduce: $$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x\,f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dy\,dx = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x\,f_X(x)\,dx = E[X]$$ $$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} y\,f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dy\,dx = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} y\,f_Y(y)\,dy = E[Y]$$ $$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dy\,dx = 1$$ **Step 4 — Combine.** $$E[aX + bY + c] = aE[X] + bE[Y] + c \cdot 1 = aE[X] + bE[Y] + c \qquad \blacksquare$$ > [!NOTE] > This proof **never used the independence of $X$ and $Y$**. Linearity of expectation is *universal* — a fact that is the most-tested concept in KTU probability questions. ### 3.3 Derivation: Variance of a Linear Combination **Claim:** $\text{Var}(aX + bY) = a^2\text{Var}(X) + b^2\text{Var}(Y) + 2ab\,\text{Cov}(X,Y)$. **Step 1 — Start from the definition of variance.** $$\text{Var}(aX + bY) = E\left[(aX + bY - E[aX + bY])^2\right]$$ **Step 2 — Use linearity to simplify the inner mean.** $$E[aX + bY] = aE[X] + bE[Y]$$ Therefore: $$\text{Var}(aX + bY) = E\left[(aX + bY - aE[X] - bE[Y])^2\right] = E\left[(a(X - E[X]) + b(Y - E[Y]))^2\right]$$ **Step 3 — Expand the square.** $$\text{Var}(aX + bY) = E\left[a^2(X - E[X])^2 + 2ab(X - E[X])(Y - E[Y]) + b^2(Y - E[Y])^2\right]$$ **Step 4 — Apply linearity of expectation and pull out constants.** $$\text{Var}(aX + bY) = a^2\,E[(X - E[X])^2] + 2ab\,E[(X - E[X])(Y - E[Y])] + b^2\,E[(Y - E[Y])^2]$$ **Step 5 — Recognize the standard quantities.** $$= a^2\,\text{Var}(X) + 2ab\,\text{Cov}(X,Y) + b^2\,\text{Var}(Y) \qquad \blacksquare$$ > [!IMPORTANT] > **If $X$ and $Y$ are independent**, $\text{Cov}(X,Y) = 0$ and the variance **adds** in quadrature: > $$\text{Var}(aX + bY) = a^2\,\text{Var}(X) + b^2\,\text{Var}(Y)$$ ### 3.4 Worked Example: Computing $E[g(X,Y)]$ for a Specific Joint PDF **Problem Setup.** Let $X$ and $Y$ have the joint PDF: $$f_{X,Y}(x,y) = \begin{cases} k(x + y) & \text{for } 0 \leq x \leq 1,\; 0 \leq y \leq 1 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$ **Step A — Find $k$ using normalization.** $$1 = \int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{1} k(x+y)\,dx\,dy$$ Compute the inner integral: $$\int_{0}^{1} (x + y)\,dx = \left[\frac{x^2}{2} + xy\right]_{x=0}^{x=1} = \frac{1}{2} + y$$ Then the outer integral: $$\int_{0}^{1} \left(\frac{1}{2} + y\right) dy = \left[\frac{y}{2} + \frac{y^2}{2}\right]_{0}^{1} = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} = 1$$ Therefore $k = 1$, and $f_{X,Y}(x,y) = x + y$ on the unit square. **Step B — Compute $E[X]$.** (By symmetry of the PDF, $E[X] = E[Y]$.) $$E[X] = \int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{1} x\,(x+y)\,dy\,dx = \int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{1} (x^2 + xy)\,dy\,dx$$ Inner integral over $y$: $$\int_{0}^{1} (x^2 + xy)\,dy = \left[x^2 y + \frac{xy^2}{2}\right]_{0}^{1} = x^2 + \frac{x}{2}$$ Outer integral over $x$: $$\int_{0}^{1} \left(x^2 + \frac{x}{2}\right) dx = \left[\frac{x^3}{3} + \frac{x^2}{4}\right]_{0}^{1} = \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{4} = \frac{7}{12}$$ **Step C — Compute $E[XY]$.** $$E[XY] = \int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{1} xy\,(x+y)\,dy\,dx = \int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{1} (x^2 y + xy^2)\,dy\,dx$$ Inner integral over $y$: $$\int_{0}^{1} (x^2 y + xy^2)\,dy = \left[\frac{x^2 y^2}{2} + \frac{xy^3}{3}\right]_{0}^{1} = \frac{x^2}{2} + \frac{x}{3}$$ Outer integral over $x$: $$\int_{0}^{1} \left(\frac{x^2}{2} + \frac{x}{3}\right) dx = \left[\frac{x^3}{6} + \frac{x^2}{6}\right]_{0}^{1} = \frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{3}$$ **Step D — Compute $\text{Cov}(X,Y)$.** $$\text{Cov}(X,Y) = E[XY] - E[X]\,E[Y] = \frac{1}{3} - \frac{7}{12} \cdot \frac{7}{12} = \frac{1}{3} - \frac{49}{144}$$ Common denominator (144): $$\text{Cov}(X,Y) = \frac{48}{144} - \frac{49}{144} = -\frac{1}{144}$$ > [!NOTE] > The negative covariance indicates that $X$ and $Y$ are **mildly negatively correlated** in this distribution. They are **not independent**, since $f_{X,Y}(x,y) = x + y \neq f_X(x)\cdot f_Y(y)$. **Step E — Compute $E[2X - 3Y + 5]$ (using linearity).** $$E[2X - 3Y + 5] = 2 \cdot \frac{7}{12} - 3 \cdot \frac{7}{12} + 5 = -\frac{7}{12} + 5 = \frac{-7 + 60}{12} = \frac{53}{12} \approx 4.4167$$ ## 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics ### 4.1 Functional Architecture Flow: Computing $E[g(X,Y)]$ The following Mermaid block diagram illustrates the **operational pipeline** a student must follow when solving a KTU-level problem on $E[g(X,Y)]$. ```mermaid flowchart TD startA[Start: Problem Given] --> nodeB{Is joint PDF fXY specified?} nodeB -- No --> nodeC[Derive fXY from CDF or geometric context] nodeB -- Yes --> nodeD[Validate: Integral equals 1, fXY greater or equal 0] nodeC --> nodeD nodeD --> nodeE{Region of integration: R2 or bounded region R?} nodeE -- Whole plane --> nodeF[Set limits to -inf to +inf] nodeE -- Bounded region --> nodeG[Identify region bounds for x and y] nodeF --> nodeH nodeG --> nodeH[Substitute g x y and fXY x y into double integral] nodeH --> nodeI[Choose order: dy then dx OR dx then dy] nodeI --> nodeJ[Evaluate inner integral keeping outer variable constant] nodeJ --> nodeK[Evaluate outer integral] nodeK --> nodeL[Apply linearity, symmetry, or independence if applicable] nodeL --> nodeM[Simplify to obtain final scalar value] nodeM --> nodeN[Cross-check: E of a constant equals the constant] nodeN --> endA[End: Report E of g X Y] style startA fill:#FFD700,stroke:#000,color:#000 style endA fill:#90EE90,stroke:#000,color:#000 style nodeB fill:#87CEEB,stroke:#000,color:#000 style nodeD fill:#FFB6C1,stroke:#000,color:#000 style nodeE fill:#DDA0DD,stroke:#000,color:#000 style nodeH fill:#F0E68C,stroke:#000,color:#000 style nodeM fill:#98FB98,stroke:#000,color:#000 ``` ### 4.2 Schematic: Three-Phase Decomposition of a Joint PDF ```mermaid flowchart LR phaseA["Phase 1: Region Identification
Define support region R in xy-plane"] phaseB["Phase 2: Density Assignment
Assign fXY x y on region R"] phaseC["Phase 3: Normalization
Solve for constant k using double integral equals 1"] phaseA --> phaseB phaseB --> phaseC phaseC --> phaseD["Ready for Moment Computation
E of g X Y etc."] style phaseA fill:#FFE4B5,stroke:#000,color:#000 style phaseB fill:#FFE4B5,stroke:#000,color:#000 style phaseC fill:#FFE4B5,stroke:#000,color:#000 style phaseD fill:#B0E0E6,stroke:#000,color:#000 ``` ### 4.3 Concept Map: Relationships Among the Key Quantities ```mermaid flowchart TD joint["Joint PDF fXY x y"] margX["Marginal fX x"] margY["Marginal fY y"] EX["E of X"] EY["E of Y"] EXY["E of XY"] VarX["Var of X"] VarY["Var of Y"] Cov["Cov of X and Y"] Corr["Correlation rho"] VarComb["Var of aX plus bY"] joint -->|integrate over y| margX joint -->|integrate over x| margY margX --> EX margY --> EY margX --> VarX margY --> VarY joint --> EXY EXY --> Cov EX --> Cov EY --> Cov Cov --> Corr VarX --> Corr VarY --> Corr Cov --> VarComb VarX --> VarComb VarY --> VarComb style joint fill:#FF6347,stroke:#000,color:#FFF style Cov fill:#FFD700,stroke:#000,color:#000 style VarComb fill:#90EE90,stroke:#000,color:#000 ``` > [!TIP] > The concept map above is a **high-yield revision tool**. Trace the arrows in reverse to understand *how* to compute each quantity from the joint PDF. ## 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap ### Part A Questions (3 Marks Each) --- **Q1. [KTU University Exam – Dec 2023]** **State the formula for the expected value of a function $g(X, Y)$ of two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint probability density function $f_{X,Y}(x,y)$. Mention the necessary condition for the formula to be valid.** **Model Answer (3 Marks):** The expected value of a function $g(X, Y)$ is defined as: $$E[g(X,Y)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x,y)\,f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dx\,dy$$ **Necessary condition:** The double integral must converge absolutely, i.e., $$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \vert g(x,y) \vert\,f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dx\,dy < \infty$$ *(1 mark for formula, 1 mark for explanation of variables, 1 mark for convergence condition.)* --- **Q2. [KTU University Exam – May 2024]** **If $X$ and $Y$ are two independent continuous random variables with marginal PDFs $f_X(x)$ and $f_Y(y)$, write down the formula for $E[XY]$ and hence state the independence property of expectation.** **Model Answer (3 Marks):** When $X$ and $Y$ are independent, the joint PDF factorizes: $f_{X,Y}(x,y) = f_X(x)\,f_Y(y)$. Substituting into the general formula: $$E[XY] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} xy\,f_X(x)\,f_Y(y)\,dx\,dy = \left[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x\,f_X(x)\,dx\right]\left[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} y\,f_Y(y)\,dy\right]$$ Therefore: $$E[XY] = E[X]\,E[Y]$$ **Independence property of expectation:** *If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, the expected value of their product equals the product of their expected values.* (1 mark for the joint PDF factorization, 1 mark for the double integral, 1 mark for the final identity and statement.) --- ### Part B Questions (14 Marks Each) > [!NOTE] > Per KTU 2024 ESE (End Semester Evaluation) regulations, you must answer **only one** of the two alternatives. Both choices are designed to test the same Course Outcome at the **Apply / Analyze** level of Revised Bloom's Taxonomy. --- ### Question A (14 Marks) **[KTU University Exam – Model Question, KTU 2024 Scheme]** The joint probability density function of two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by: $$f_{X,Y}(x,y) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{x + y}{3} & \text{for } 0 \leq x \leq 1,\; 0 \leq y \leq 2 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$ **Part (a) [7 Marks]:** Verify that $f_{X,Y}(x,y)$ is a valid joint PDF. Hence find $E[X]$, $E[Y]$, and $E[X + Y]$. **Part (b) [7 Marks]:** Find $E[XY]$ and hence compute $\text{Cov}(X,Y)$ and the correlation coefficient $\rho_{X,Y}$. Comment on whether $X$ and $Y$ are independent. --- **Complete Model Solution:** #### Part (a) Solution **Step 1 — Verify the joint PDF.** We need: - (i) $f_{X,Y}(x,y) \geq 0$ on the support, and - (ii) $\int\int f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dx\,dy = 1$. For (i): On the region $0 \leq x \leq 1,\; 0 \leq y \leq 2$, both $x \geq 0$ and $y \geq 0$, so $x + y \geq 0$. Thus $f_{X,Y} \geq 0$. ✓ For (ii): $$\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{2} \frac{x + y}{3}\,dy\,dx$$ Inner integral: $$\int_{0}^{2} (x + y)\,dy = \left[xy + \frac{y^2}{2}\right]_{0}^{2} = 2x + 2$$ Outer integral: $$\int_{0}^{1} \frac{2x + 2}{3}\,dx = \frac{1}{3}\left[x^2 + 2x\right]_{0}^{1} = \frac{1}{3}(1 + 2) = 1 \;\checkmark$$ The joint PDF is **valid**. (2 marks for verification) **Step 2 — Compute $E[X]$.** $$E[X] = \int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{2} x \cdot \frac{x + y}{3}\,dy\,dx = \frac{1}{3}\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{2} (x^2 + xy)\,dy\,dx$$ Inner: $$\int_{0}^{2} (x^2 + xy)\,dy = \left[x^2 y + \frac{xy^2}{2}\right]_{0}^{2} = 2x^2 + 2x$$ Outer: $$\frac{1}{3}\int_{0}^{1} (2x^2 + 2x)\,dx = \frac{1}{3}\left[\frac{2x^3}{3} + x^2\right]_{0}^{1} = \frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{2}{3} + 1\right) = \frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{5}{3} = \frac{5}{9}$$ **Step 3 — Compute $E[Y]$.** $$E[Y] = \int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{2} y \cdot \frac{x + y}{3}\,dy\,dx = \frac{1}{3}\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{2} (xy + y^2)\,dy\,dx$$ Inner: $$\int_{0}^{2} (xy + y^2)\,dy = \left[\frac{xy^2}{2} + \frac{y^3}{3}\right]_{0}^{2} = 2x + \frac{8}{3}$$ Outer: $$\frac{1}{3}\int_{0}^{1} \left(2x + \frac{8}{3}\right) dx = \frac{1}{3}\left[x^2 + \frac{8x}{3}\right]_{0}^{1} = \frac{1}{3}\left(1 + \frac{8}{3}\right) = \frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{11}{3} = \frac{11}{9}$$ **Step 4 — Use linearity for $E[X + Y]$.** $$E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y] = \frac{5}{9} + \frac{11}{9} = \frac{16}{9}$$ *(5 marks for computing E of X, E of Y, and E of X plus Y; 2 marks reserved for the verification of the joint PDF.)* #### Part (b) Solution **Step 1 — Compute $E[XY]$.** $$E[XY] = \int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{2} xy \cdot \frac{x + y}{3}\,dy\,dx = \frac{1}{3}\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{2} (x^2 y + xy^2)\,dy\,dx$$ Inner: $$\int_{0}^{2} (x^2 y + xy^2)\,dy = \left[\frac{x^2 y^2}{2} + \frac{xy^3}{3}\right]_{0}^{2} = 2x^2 + \frac{8x}{3}$$ Outer: $$\frac{1}{3}\int_{0}^{1}\left(2x^2 + \frac{8x}{3}\right) dx = \frac{1}{3}\left[\frac{2x^3}{3} + \frac{4x^2}{3}\right]_{0}^{1} = \frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{2}{3} + \frac{4}{3}\right) = \frac{1}{3} \cdot 2 = \frac{2}{3}$$ **Step 2 — Compute $\text{Cov}(X, Y)$.** $$\text{Cov}(X,Y) = E[XY] - E[X]\,E[Y] = \frac{2}{3} - \frac{5}{9} \cdot \frac{11}{9} = \frac{2}{3} - \frac{55}{81}$$ Common denominator 81: $$\text{Cov}(X,Y) = \frac{54}{81} - \frac{55}{81} = -\frac{1}{81}$$ **Step 3 — Compute $\text{Var}(X)$ and $\text{Var}(Y)$ to find $\rho$.** $$E[X^2] = \int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{2} x^2 \cdot \frac{x + y}{3}\,dy\,dx = \frac{1}{3}\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{2} (x^3 + x^2 y)\,dy\,dx$$ Inner: $$\int_{0}^{2} (x^3 + x^2 y)\,dy = 2x^3 + 2x^2$$ Outer: $$\frac{1}{3}\int_{0}^{1} (2x^3 + 2x^2)\,dx = \frac{1}{3}\left[\frac{x^4}{2} + \frac{2x^3}{3}\right]_{0}^{1} = \frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{2}{3}\right) = \frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{7}{6} = \frac{7}{18}$$ Therefore: $$\text{Var}(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2 = \frac{7}{18} - \left(\frac{5}{9}\right)^2 = \frac{7}{18} - \frac{25}{81}$$ Common denominator 162: $$\text{Var}(X) = \frac{63}{162} - \frac{50}{162} = \frac{13}{162}$$ $$E[Y^2] = \int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{2} y^2 \cdot \frac{x + y}{3}\,dy\,dx = \frac{1}{3}\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{2} (xy^2 + y^3)\,dy\,dx$$ Inner: $$\int_{0}^{2} (xy^2 + y^3)\,dy = \left[\frac{xy^3}{3} + \frac{y^4}{4}\right]_{0}^{2} = \frac{8x}{3} + 4$$ Outer: $$\frac{1}{3}\int_{0}^{1}\left(\frac{8x}{3} + 4\right) dx = \frac{1}{3}\left[\frac{4x^2}{3} + 4x\right]_{0}^{1} = \frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{4}{3} + 4\right) = \frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{16}{3} = \frac{16}{9}$$ Therefore: $$\text{Var}(Y) = E[Y^2] - (E[Y])^2 = \frac{16}{9} - \left(\frac{11}{9}\right)^2 = \frac{16}{9} - \frac{121}{81}$$ Common denominator 81: $$\text{Var}(Y) = \frac{144}{81} - \frac{121}{81} = \frac{23}{81}$$ **Step 4 — Compute $\rho_{X,Y}$.** $$\rho_{X,Y} = \frac{\text{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sqrt{\text{Var}(X)\,\text{Var}(Y)}} = \frac{-1/81}{\sqrt{(13/162)(23/81)}}$$ Compute the denominator: $$\text{Var}(X)\,\text{Var}(Y) = \frac{13}{162} \cdot \frac{23}{81} = \frac{13 \cdot 23}{162 \cdot 81} = \frac{299}{13122}$$ $$\sqrt{\frac{299}{13122}} \approx \sqrt{0.02278} \approx 0.1509$$ $$\rho_{X,Y} \approx \frac{-0.01235}{0.1509} \approx -0.0818$$ **Step 5 — Comment on independence.** Since $\rho_{X,Y} \neq 0$ (it is approximately $-0.082$), $X$ and $Y$ are **not linearly uncorrelated**, which means they cannot be independent. Additionally, the joint PDF $f_{X,Y}(x,y) = \frac{x+y}{3}$ does **not** factor into $f_X(x)\cdot f_Y(y)$ (one can verify that $f_X(x) = \frac{2x+2}{3}$ and $f_Y(y) = \frac{y+2}{3}$ — their product is not equal to the original $f_{X,Y}$). **Therefore, $X$ and $Y$ are NOT independent.** *(4 marks for E of XY and Cov; 3 marks for variances, correlation, and the independence comment.)* --- ### Question B (14 Marks) — *Internal Choice Alternative* **[KTU University Exam – Model Question, KTU 2024 Scheme]** Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with joint PDF: $$f_{X,Y}(x,y) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{xy}{9} & \text{for } 0 \leq x \leq 2,\; 0 \leq y \leq 3 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$ **Part (a) [7 Marks]:** Verify the joint PDF, then find $E[2X + 3Y - 4]$, $E[X^2]$, and $E[Y^2]$. **Part (b) [7 Marks]:** Find $E[XY]$, $\text{Cov}(X,Y)$, $\text{Var}(2X - 3Y)$, and the correlation coefficient $\rho_{X,Y}$. State whether $X$ and $Y$ are independent. --- **Complete Model Solution:** #### Part (a) Solution **Step 1 — Verify joint PDF.** (i) On the support, $x \geq 0$ and $y \geq 0$, so $f_{X,Y} = \frac{xy}{9} \geq 0$. ✓ (ii) Normalization check: $$\int_{0}^{2}\int_{0}^{3} \frac{xy}{9}\,dy\,dx = \frac{1}{9}\int_{0}^{2} x \left[\frac{y^2}{2}\right]_{0}^{3} dx = \frac{1}{9}\int_{0}^{2} x \cdot \frac{9}{2}\,dx = \frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{2} x\,dx = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 2 = 1 \;\checkmark$$ **Step 2 — Compute $E[X]$ and $E[Y]$ (needed for linearity).** $$E[X] = \int_{0}^{2}\int_{0}^{3} x \cdot \frac{xy}{9}\,dy\,dx = \frac{1}{9}\int_{0}^{2}\int_{0}^{3} x^2 y\,dy\,dx = \frac{1}{9}\int_{0}^{2} x^2 \cdot \frac{9}{2}\,dx = \frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{2} x^2\,dx = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{8}{3} = \frac{4}{3}$$ $$E[Y] = \int_{0}^{2}\int_{0}^{3} y \cdot \frac{xy}{9}\,dy\,dx = \frac{1}{9}\int_{0}^{2} x \cdot \frac{27}{2}\,dx = \frac{3}{2}\int_{0}^{2} x\,dx = \frac{3}{2} \cdot 2 = 3$$ **Step 3 — Apply linearity for $E[2X + 3Y - 4]$.** $$E[2X + 3Y - 4] = 2 \cdot \frac{4}{3} + 3 \cdot 3 - 4 = \frac{8}{3} + 9 - 4 = \frac{8}{3} + 5 = \frac{8 + 15}{3} = \frac{23}{3}$$ **Step 4 — Compute $E[X^2]$ and $E[Y^2]$.** $$E[X^2] = \int_{0}^{2}\int_{0}^{3} x^2 \cdot \frac{xy}{9}\,dy\,dx = \frac{1}{9}\int_{0}^{2} x^3 \cdot \frac{9}{2}\,dx = \frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{2} x^3\,dx = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 4 = 2$$ $$E[Y^2] = \int_{0}^{2}\int_{0}^{3} y^2 \cdot \frac{xy}{9}\,dy\,dx = \frac{1}{9}\int_{0}^{2} x \cdot \frac{81}{2}\,dx = \frac{9}{2}\int_{0}^{2} x\,dx = \frac{9}{2} \cdot 2 = 9$$ *(2 marks for verification; 3 marks for E of 2X plus 3Y minus 4 via linearity; 2 marks for second moments.)* #### Part (b) Solution **Step 1 — Compute $E[XY]$.** $$E[XY] = \int_{0}^{2}\int_{0}^{3} xy \cdot \frac{xy}{9}\,dy\,dx = \frac{1}{9}\int_{0}^{2} x^2 \cdot \frac{27}{2}\,dx = \frac{3}{2}\int_{0}^{2} x^2\,dx = \frac{3}{2} \cdot \frac{8}{3} = 4$$ **Step 2 — Compute $\text{Cov}(X, Y)$.** $$\text{Cov}(X,Y) = E[XY] - E[X]\,E[Y] = 4 - \frac{4}{3} \cdot 3 = 4 - 4 = 0$$ **Step 3 — Compute $\text{Var}(X)$ and $\text{Var}(Y)$.** $$\text{Var}(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2 = 2 - \frac{16}{9} = \frac{18 - 16}{9} = \frac{2}{9}$$ $$\text{Var}(Y) = E[Y^2] - (E[Y])^2 = 9 - 9 = 0$$ **Step 4 — Compute $\text{Var}(2X - 3Y)$.** Using the formula $\text{Var}(aX + bY) = a^2\text{Var}(X) + b^2\text{Var}(Y) + 2ab\,\text{Cov}(X,Y)$ with $a = 2$, $b = -3$: $$\text{Var}(2X - 3Y) = 4 \cdot \frac{2}{9} + 9 \cdot 0 + 2(2)(-3) \cdot 0 = \frac{8}{9}$$ **Step 5 — Compute $\rho_{X,Y}$.** $$\rho_{X,Y} = \frac{\text{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sqrt{\text{Var}(X)\,\text{Var}(Y)}}$$ Since $\text{Var}(Y) = 0$ (i.e., $Y$ is **degenerate**, taking the constant value 3 almost surely), the denominator is 0 and $\rho_{X,Y}$ is **undefined**. **Step 6 — Independence check.** Although $\text{Cov}(X,Y) = 0$ would normally suggest independence, here $Y$ is degenerate (constant 3), so the question of independence is vacuous. We can verify factorization: $$f_X(x) = \int_{0}^{3} \frac{xy}{9}\,dy = \frac{x}{9} \cdot \frac{9}{2} = \frac{x}{2}, \quad 0 \leq x \leq 2$$ $$f_Y(y) = \int_{0}^{2} \frac{xy}{9}\,dx = \frac{y}{9} \cdot 2 = \frac{2y}{9}, \quad 0 \leq y \leq 3$$ Then $f_X(x) \cdot f_Y(y) = \frac{x}{2} \cdot \frac{2y}{9} = \frac{xy}{9} = f_{X,Y}(x,y)$. ✓ **Therefore, $X$ and $Y$ are independent in this case.** This is a beautiful illustration that independence ⇔ factorization of the joint PDF, not merely zero covariance. *(3 marks for E of XY and Cov; 2 marks for Var of 2X minus 3Y using the formula; 2 marks for correlation, independence, and factorization check.)* --- > [!WARNING] > **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Common Pitfalls:** > 1. **Forgetting normalization:** Many students use the given $f_{X,Y}$ without verifying that the double integral equals 1. The constant $k$ must be solved for **first**. (1–2 mark deduction) > 2. **Confusing independence with zero covariance:** For **non-Gaussian** distributions, $\text{Cov} = 0$ does **not** imply independence. Always verify via $f_{X,Y} = f_X \cdot f_Y$. > 3. **Order of integration:** When the region is not a simple rectangle, drawing the region and choosing the correct limits is critical. Marks are awarded for **setting up**, not just the final answer. > 4. **Linear combination variance formula:** A frequent error is writing $\text{Var}(aX + bY) = a^2\text{Var}(X) + b^2\text{Var}(Y)$ without checking independence. If $X$ and $Y$ are dependent, the $2ab\,\text{Cov}(X,Y)$ term must be included. > 5. **Units and dimensions:** Although rare, examiners may deduct marks if the integrand's units are inconsistent with the resulting expectation's units. --- ### Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember (Rapid Revision Checklist) - [x] **Master Formula:** $E[g(X,Y)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x,y)\,f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dx\,dy$. - [x] **Validity Conditions:** $f_{X,Y}(x,y) \geq 0$ everywhere and the double integral equals **1**. - [x] **Linearity of Expectation** is **universal** — no independence assumption needed for $E[aX + bY + c]$. - [x] **Multiplicativity** ($E[XY] = E[X]E[Y]$) requires **independence**, not merely zero covariance. - [x] **Covariance Identity:** $\text{Cov}(X,Y) = E[XY] - E[X]\,E[Y]$ is the most-used formula in KTU problems. - [x] **Variance Combination:** $\text{Var}(aX + bY) = a^2\text{Var}(X) + b^2\text{Var}(Y) + 2ab\,\text{Cov}(X,Y)$. - [x] **Correlation Bound:** $\rho_{X,Y} \in [-1, +1]$; undefined if either variance is zero. - [x] **Independence Test:** Check $f_{X,Y}(x,y) = f_X(x) \cdot f_Y(y)$ on the support. - [x] **Marginal Recovery:** $f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dy$ is how 2D moments reduce to 1D moments. - [x] **Symmetry Trick:** If $f_{X,Y}(x,y) = f_{X,Y}(y,x)$ (symmetric in $x$ and $y$), then $E[X] = E[Y]$ and $E[X^2] = E[Y^2]$. - [x] **KTU Pattern:** Questions typically bundle **joint PDF validation** + **means** + **second moments** + **covariance/correlation** in a single 14-mark problem. - [x] **Convergence Caveat:** If $\int\int \vert g(x,y) \vert f_{X,Y}\,dx\,dy = \infty$, the expectation $E[g(X,Y)]$ **does not exist**.
